++{"role": "user", "id": "msg_9093cbd1-176d-4e22-a9e2-a9fbe6c91de9", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_result": {"name": "skill", "tool_use_id": "call_YjVvTW4H63yijKFJo3QHaLoM", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Launching skill: html-authoring\n\n<command-message>The \"html-authoring\" skill is running</command-message>\n<command-name>html-authoring</command-name>\n\nSKILL.md: /Users/skodi/.local/share/cortex/1.2.42+191048.079d099b54b5/bundled_skills/html-authoring/SKILL.md\nBase directory: /Users/skodi/.local/share/cortex/1.2.42+191048.079d099b54b5/bundled_skills/html-authoring\n\n# HTML Authoring\n\nWhen report sharing is enabled, Snowflake renders your report HTML in a **locked-down sandbox**: a strict Content-Security-Policy applies and the page has **no network access**. Author to the rules below so the report renders correctly and is safe to share — plain, self-contained HTML with inline JavaScript and all data embedded is ideal.\n\n---\n\n## Where to save the file\n\n**Never leave the file in transient storage** — a temporary or scratch location (e.g. `/tmp`) is wiped when the session ends, leaving nothing to publish or refresh later. The file must land somewhere durable.\n\n**When a workspace is mounted:** save a new report to the **current workspace**. If the user names another durable destination, use that. If no durable destination is clear, ask before writing.\n\n**Cowork:** `/workspace` is the sandbox thread directory. It is not the user's personal workspace, and it is not a workspace they have open in Snowsight. Write the `.html` file under `/workspace` and present that file in the chat. Do not use the term Workspace when communicating about the saved location.\n\n**No workspace mounted, and this is not Cowork:** ask where to save the file before writing. Do not invent a destination, and do not treat a local directory as the user's workspace.\n\n**Updating an existing report:** write it back to the same location. An existing file may predate these rules, so before saving **any** edit — even a one-line change — check the whole file against this list and fix what fails:\n\n1. `<head>` has the `snowflake-source` marker meta tag and the viewport tag.\n2. A metadata block exists (add one if it is missing), with a `sections[]` entry keyed to each section's anchor id — including any section you added (give it an id).\n3. Nothing from **Don't use** below remains — in particular no inline event handlers, no CDN or remote scripts, stylesheets, fonts or images, and no runtime network or storage calls.\n4. Colors adapt to light and dark (`color-scheme` + `light-dark()`, or a `prefers-color-scheme` block).\n5. Every `<table>` sits inside an `overflow-x: auto` wrapper.\n\n**Publishing:** to publish HTML as a CoWork artifact, load `snowflake-publish-report`. Do not invent a share flow. After creating or editing a report, end your reply by asking whether to publish it; if it is already published, say the published version does not include your changes yet. Do not publish or republish until the user confirms.\n\n---\n\n## Marker meta tag\n\nInclude this in `<head>` so downstream tooling knows the file is agent-authored:\n\n```html\n<meta name=\"snowflake-source\" content=\"cortex-agent-authored\">\n```\n\n---\n\n## Report metadata — for later refresh\n\nEmbed one provenance block in `<head>` so a future run (yours or another agent's) can **refresh or iterate** on the report — its equivalent of a header doc-comment in code. Record where the data came from and how each part was produced. It's a `<script type=\"application/json\">` data block: never rendered, never executed (wrong type), and read by **parsing, not position** — so it stays intact if the pipeline lifts it into a manifest.\n\n```html\n<script type=\"application/json\" id=\"snowflake-report-metadata\">\n{\n  \"generated\": \"2026-06-23\",\n  \"intent\": \"Q4 revenue analysis by region\",\n  \"dataSources\": [\n    { \"type\": \"query\", \"warehouse\": \"{WAREHOUSE}\",\n      \"sql\": \"SELECT region, SUM(revenue) AS revenue FROM {DATABASE}.{SCHEMA}.{TABLE} WHERE quarter = 'Q4' GROUP BY region\" }\n  ],\n  \"sections\": [\n    { \"id\": \"revenue-by-region\", \"title\": \"Revenue by region\",\n      \"dataSources\": [{ \"type\": \"query\", \"sql\": \"SELECT region, SUM(revenue) … GROUP BY region\" }],\n      \"producerNotes\": \"Chart values are inlined from the query above — re-run it to refresh.\" }\n  ]\n}\n</script>\n```\n\n- **Key each `sections[]` entry to the section's anchor id** (`<h2 id=\"revenue-by-region\">` or `<section id=\"…\">`). The id — not the block's position — is the link, so \"refresh section X\" is a lookup on `sections[].id`, and the pipeline can extract the whole block without losing which entry maps to which section.\n- Scope each source: put it in a section's `dataSources` if it feeds only that section, or in the top-level `dataSources` if it's shared across sections — use either or both. (The template below is section-level only because each source is section-specific.)\n- Keep it machine-readable: list every query / table / file each part draws on, plus any parameters or assumptions a future update needs.\n- **Record every query as `{ \"type\": \"query\", \"sql\": \"<the SQL text>\" }` in a `dataSources` array** — the SQL itself, never under another key (such as `query` or `originalQuery`) and never as a path to a `.sql` file. That includes the query that produced a file you were given: add a `query` source with the SQL copied in, alongside a `{ \"type\": \"file\", \"path\": \"…\" }` source for the file. Keeping every query in the same place and shape lets a later run, or a script, find them all.\n- Update it whenever you change what the report shows.\n- Tokens in `{…}` (e.g. `{DATABASE}.{SCHEMA}.{TABLE}`) are placeholders — replace them with the report's real fully-qualified sources.\n- Include only fields you know. `\"warehouse\"` is optional: record it when a warehouse was actually used or named, and delete the field when none was. Omit any other field whose value you don't have too. Never leave a `{…}` token in the saved file.\n\n---\n\n## What you can and can't use\n\n**Use freely:**\n- ✅ Inline `<script>` — put all your JavaScript here.\n- ✅ Inline `<style>` and `style=\"…\"` attributes.\n- ✅ `<canvas>`, inline `<svg>`, and the vendored `/libs/` libraries (below).\n- ✅ Images as `data:` or `blob:` URIs.\n\n**Don't use** (silently dropped or blocked):\n- ❌ Inline event handlers (`onclick=`, `onload=`, …) — attach handlers with `addEventListener` inside a `<script>`.\n- ❌ `eval`, `new Function`, or `setTimeout(\"…code…\")`.\n- ❌ External / CDN scripts, stylesheets, or web fonts — load only from `/libs/`.\n- ❌ Remote images (`<img src=\"https://…\">`) — inline the bytes as a `data:` URI.\n- ❌ Runtime network calls — `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `sendBeacon`. Embed all data directly in the HTML.\n- ❌ Cookies, `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` — unavailable in the sandbox.\n- ❌ `<iframe>`, `<object>`/`<embed>`, `<video>`/`<audio>`, Web Workers, `<form>` submission, `<base>`.\n\n---\n\n## Available libraries\n\nReference a vendored library by its **pinned path** — nothing else loads:\n\n```html\n<script src=\"/libs/chart.js@4.4.4/chart.umd.js\"></script>\n<link rel=\"stylesheet\" href=\"/libs/katex@0.16.21/katex.min.css\">\n```\n\n| Library | Reference path | Use / limits |\n|---|---|---|\n| chart.js | `/libs/chart.js@4.4.4/chart.umd.js` | Charts (renders to `<canvas>`) |\n| plotly (cartesian) | `/libs/plotly.js-cartesian-dist-min@2.35.2/plotly-cartesian.min.js` | Cartesian charts only |\n| d3 | `/libs/d3@7.9.0/d3.min.js` | Low-level data viz |\n| vega | `/libs/vega@6.2.0/vega.min.js` | Base for vega-lite / vega-embed |\n| vega-lite | `/libs/vega-lite@6.4.3/vega-lite.min.js` | Declarative charts |\n| vega-embed | `/libs/vega-embed@7.1.0/vega-embed.min.js` | Embeds a spec — **must** pass `{ ast: true }` |\n| mermaid | `/libs/mermaid@10.9.6/mermaid.min.js` | Diagrams (flowchart, sequence, class, state, ER, gantt, pie, gitGraph, journey, …) — **must init with `securityLevel: 'strict'`** |\n| katex | `/libs/katex@0.16.21/katex.min.js` + `/libs/katex@0.16.21/katex.min.css` | Math typesetting |\n| highlight.js | `/libs/highlight.js@11.10.0/highlight.min.js` + `/libs/highlight.js@11.10.0/github.min.css` | Code highlighting |\n| marked | `/libs/marked@14.1.3/marked.min.js` | Markdown → HTML |\n| three | `/libs/three@0.169.0/three.module.min.js` | 3D (WebGL); ES module |\n\nNotes:\n- **Mermaid:** initialize with `securityLevel: 'strict'` (required — it sanitizes diagram labels; never use `'loose'`). Images in labels must be `data:` URIs or inline `<svg>` — remote image URLs are blocked and won't load.\n- **Vega:** always pass `{ ast: true }` to `vegaEmbed` (required — without it the chart won't render). Give the spec an explicit numeric `width` (e.g. `width: 700`) — `width: 'container'` renders a zero-width, blank chart in the sandbox.\n- **KaTeX:** include both the JS and the CSS.\n- **three.js** is an ES module — load it with `<script type=\"module\">`.\n\n---\n\n## Theming (light & dark)\n\nReports adapt to the viewer's light or dark color scheme, so **make your CSS adapt too** — don't hard-code a light background with dark text (or vice-versa).\n\n- Use the `light-dark()` function for colors, e.g. `color: light-dark(#1f2937, #e5e7eb);`, and declare `:root { color-scheme: light dark; }`.\n- Or provide `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { … }` overrides.\n\n---\n\n## Responsive layout\n\nReports are opened on phones and in narrow side-panels as often as full-width, so the layout must **reflow, not overflow** — nothing should force horizontal page scrolling or spill past the viewport edge on a ~360px-wide screen. The `<meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width, initial-scale=1\">` tag (in the template) is what makes this possible — always keep it.\n\n- **Fluid container:** cap the width but let it shrink — `max-width: 880px; width: 100%; box-sizing: border-box;` — and use fluid padding like `padding: clamp(16px, 4vw, 24px);` so narrow screens aren't cramped and wide ones aren't sparse.\n- **Wide tables:** wrap every table in a horizontally scrollable container so the table scrolls on its own instead of stretching the whole page:\n  ```html\n  <div style=\"overflow-x: auto;\"><table>…</table></div>\n  ```\n- **Images & SVG:** add `img, svg { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }` so they never exceed the viewport width.\n- **Charts (chart.js):** wrap the `<canvas>` in a **fixed-height box** and let the chart fill it — put the height in CSS, never let the chart's own aspect ratio decide it. A ratio that looks right on desktop (e.g. a `1040×360` canvas, or `aspectRatio`/`height:auto` derived from it) collapses to a short unreadable sliver at phone width. See the pattern below (`.chart-box` + `responsive: true, maintainAspectRatio: false`). For Vega-Lite, `width: 'container'` renders blank in the sandbox, so keep a numeric `width` and wrap the chart in `<div style=\"overflow-x: auto;\">` so it scrolls when the screen is narrower than the chart.\n- **Charts (Plotly):** Plotly renders to a `<div>`, so the `.chart-box`/canvas pattern doesn't apply. Wrap it in a `width: 100%` container, set `layout: { autosize: true }` (no fixed `width`), and pass `{ responsive: true }` as the config to `Plotly.newPlot(...)` so it re-fits when the viewport changes.\n- **Avoid fixed pixel widths** on layout elements — prefer `%`, `max-width`, and `min()`/`clamp()`. For multi-column layouts use a grid/flex that collapses on narrow screens, e.g. `display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr));` or `display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap;`.\n- **Test narrow:** picture the report at ~360px wide — if anything is cut off or triggers horizontal scrolling of the whole page, constrain or wrap it.\n\n---\n\n## External links\n\nWrite normal links with real URLs:\n\n```html\n<a href=\"https://docs.snowflake.com/\">Docs</a>\n```\n\n- Hrefs with embedded userinfo (`https://user@host/…`) or a protocol-relative form (`//host/…`) are made inert — the text stays, but they aren't clickable.\n- `mailto:` and `tel:` links are kept as-is — use them for contact links.\n- Don't use `javascript:` or `data:` hrefs (they're stripped), and don't rely on JavaScript (`window.open`, `location = …`) to navigate.\n\n---\n\n## Charts & interactivity — the pattern\n\nPut all logic in an inline `<script>` and load the library from `/libs/`.\n\n**chart.js** — wrap the `<canvas>` in a fixed-height box and let the chart fill it. The box's CSS height controls the chart height at every screen width; `maintainAspectRatio: false` lets it span the full width:\n\n```html\n<style>\n  .chart-box { position: relative; width: 100%; height: 320px; }   /* height lives here */\n  .chart-box > canvas { width: 100% !important; height: 100% !important; }\n</style>\n<div class=\"chart-box\"><canvas id=\"rev\"></canvas></div>    <!-- no width/height attrs on the canvas -->\n<script src=\"/libs/chart.js@4.4.4/chart.umd.js\"></script>\n<script>\n  new Chart(document.getElementById('rev'), {\n    type: 'bar',\n    data: {\n      labels: ['North America', 'EMEA', 'APAC'],\n      datasets: [{ label: 'Revenue ($M)', data: [1.2, 0.5, 0.4] }],\n    },\n    options: { responsive: true, maintainAspectRatio: false },   // fill the box\n  });\n</script>\n```\n\n> This is the sizing that survives a narrow screen. **Don't** size a chart by its canvas `width`/`height` attributes or by `aspectRatio`/`height: auto` — a wide desktop ratio (e.g. `1040×360`) collapses to a ~100px-tall sliver at phone width. Pinning the height on `.chart-box` and filling it (`maintainAspectRatio: false`) gives a full-width, controlled-height chart on every device; the `.chart-box > canvas` rule keeps it filling the box even if the runtime strips chart.js's inline sizing. For a taller/shorter chart, change the one `height` value (use `clamp()`, e.g. `height: clamp(240px, 45vw, 360px)`, if you want it to grow a little on wider screens).\n\n**Vega-Lite** (always pass `{ ast: true }`):\n\n```html\n<div id=\"vis\"></div>\n<script src=\"/libs/vega@6.2.0/vega.min.js\"></script>\n<script src=\"/libs/vega-lite@6.4.3/vega-lite.min.js\"></script>\n<script src=\"/libs/vega-embed@7.1.0/vega-embed.min.js\"></script>\n<script>\n  const spec = {\n    width: 700, height: 300,                 // numeric width — 'container' renders blank in the sandbox\n    data: { values: [{ r: 'NA', v: 1.2 }, { r: 'EMEA', v: 0.5 }, { r: 'APAC', v: 0.4 }] },\n    mark: 'bar',\n    encoding: { x: { field: 'r', type: 'nominal' }, y: { field: 'v', type: 'quantitative' } },\n  };\n  vegaEmbed('#vis', spec, { ast: true });\n</script>\n```\n\n**Mermaid** (always set `securityLevel: 'strict'`):\n\n```html\n<pre class=\"mermaid\">\nflowchart TD\n  A[Start] --> B{OK?}\n  B -->|yes| C[Done]\n</pre>\n<script src=\"/libs/mermaid@10.9.6/mermaid.min.js\"></script>\n<script>\n  mermaid.initialize({ startOnLoad: true, securityLevel: 'strict' });\n</script>\n```\n\n---\n\n## Recommended: chart details menu\n\n> **This is a recommendation, not a requirement.** It is the default for a report with data-backed charts, but the user's prompt always wins. If the user asks for no menu, different buttons, a different design, or no SQL, do that instead. If they opt out, leave it out and don't add it back when you later edit the same report.\n\nGive each **data-backed chart** (one drawn from a query or dataset you actually have) a small details menu, so a reader can check where the numbers came from without leaving the report. Skip it for illustrations, diagrams (mermaid), and charts with no source data.\n\nThe menu has four buttons that swap the chart's panel in place:\n\n| Button | Shows |\n|---|---|\n| **Chart** | The chart (the initial view). |\n| **SQL** | The query that produced the chart's data, with a **Copy** button. |\n| **Preview** | The rows the chart is drawn from, as a table. |\n| **Info** | What the chart shows, its source, how it was derived, and any caveats. |\n\nDesign rules:\n- **A pill on the chart's upper-right edge**, absolutely positioned so it takes no space in the layout. Show it on hover or keyboard focus (`:focus-within`), and keep it always visible on touch screens (`@media (hover: none)`).\n- **Match the report.** Inherit its font and use `light-dark()` colors, so the menu fits any template, light or dark.\n- **Accessible.** Real `<button type=\"button\">` elements with `aria-pressed`, handlers via `addEventListener` (no inline handlers), and a `role=\"status\"` line for \"copied\" feedback.\n- **Fixed-height panels** (same height as the chart box) so switching views doesn't shift the page.\n- **Many charts:** give each chart its own `.chart-card`; the one script below wires up all of them.\n\nContent rules:\n- **SQL and Preview must match the chart's real data** — the same query and the same rows. Never invent a query, rows, or provenance to fill the menu. Make **Info** specific (metric definition, source table, time range, filters, caveats), not generic filler.\n- **Don't show SQL if the user or an admin policy says not to.** Omit the SQL button *and* leave the SQL out of the whole file — including the metadata block, scripts, Preview and Info. A hidden panel is not access control. If the chart has no query behind it (e.g. data from an uploaded file), drop the SQL button and keep the other three.\n- Keep the SQL panel and the matching `sections[].dataSources` entry in the metadata block identical.\n- The menu uses only inline CSS/JS and no network, so it works in the sandbox. **Copy goes through `navigator.clipboard.writeText` only:** the viewer intercepts every call and shows the reader a confirmation dialog, so the promise stays pending until they choose, resolves on Allow, and rejects on Deny or dismissal. Don't treat a rejection as an error (the reader may simply have declined) and don't claim \"copied\" before it resolves; fall back to a neutral \"not copied, select the SQL manually\" message (the SQL is in a selectable `<pre>`). Don't use `document.execCommand('copy')` or `ClipboardItem`; they aren't bridged.\n\nExample (chart.js; replace the `{…}` placeholders with the chart's real source):\n\n```html\n<style>\n  .chart-card { position: relative; \\n249... <h2 id=\\\"lessons\\\">What we learned</h2>\\n250... <ol>\\n251...   <li><b>The big wins are generic.</b> Filter first, build strings late, gather only the columns that reach <code>OUT</code>, delete dead code, use TOPK. These gave 4–8.5× on q0001, q0004 and q0007. The self-join idioms win most on large data (20–47×), and they are the riskiest.</li>\\n252...   <li><b>Correctness may use constraints, never stats.</b> <code>customers</code> has no key, so assuming <code>c_id</code> is unique is a real bug, caught by the q0004 baseline.</li>\\n253...   <li><b>NULL semantics are the main trap.</b> HJOIN drops NULL keys but GROUP keeps them, and NULLIFE turns <code>''</code> into NULL.</li>\\n254...   <li><b>An operation may only run on a subset of the rows it originally ran on.</b> Removing work can only remove errors, which is allowed.</li>\\n255...   <li><b>Weak data hides bugs.</b> The example data passed two broken q0007 variants, and generated data missed a q0004 bug until literals from the programs were planted in it.</li>\\n256...   <li><b>Multiset comparison is too lenient</b> when the program sorts, and an order rule fixes it. <b>The output JSON has no types</b>, so BOOL must never equal INT, and only text in minivm's own number format may be compared as a number.</li>\\n257...   <li><b>Test the tester.</b> Zero defects proves nothing until seeded bugs are caught and honest-but-different optimizers pass.</li>\\n258...   <li><b>Measure the harness too.</b> The platform binary is 4.6× faster than the wrapper, which leaves the 2-minute budget roomy.</li>\\n259... </ol>\\n260... \\n261... <h2 id=\\\"course-corrections\\\">Course corrections</h2>\\n262... <div class=\\\"table-wrap\\\"><table>\\n263...   <thead><tr><th>When</th><th>What happened</th><th>Response</th></tr></thead>\\n264...   <tbody>\\n265...     <tr><td>#7</td><td>Two hand-optimization subagents were cancelled, and a long research pass was interrupted.</td><td>No retries. \\n249... <h2 id=\\\"lessons\\\">What we learned</h2>\\n250... <ol>\\n251...   <li><b>The big wins are generic.</b> Filter first, build strings late, gather only the columns that reach <code>OUT</code>, delete dead code, use TOPK. These gave 4–8.5× on q0001, q0004 and q0007. ++    <div class="step"><span class="n">Follow-up</span><b>Explain the session</b>Create a durable HTML mental model plus text-only exports of prompts, session files, and git history.</div>
++  </div>
++
++  <h2 id="step-by-step">Step by step mental model</h2>
++  <p>The session followed a simple review loop: understand current claims, compare them with the actual prototype, tighten the plan, then capture the record.</p>
++
++  <div class="loop">
++    <div class="loop-title">Core review loop</div>
++    <div class="flow">
++      <div class="step"><span class="n">1</span><b>Read the current state</b>Loaded the one-pager, <code>BUILD_PLAN.md</code>, MiniVM docs, and the evaluator / generator prototype files.</div>
++      <div class="step"><span class="n">2</span><b>Compare claims to evidence</b>Checked whether the build plan's claims about correctness, timing, and scale were fully backed by prototype code and docs.</div>
++      <div class="step"><span class="n">3</span><b>Find concrete gaps</b>Identified unfinished tie handling, numeric-looking string ambiguity, heuristic order detection, optimistic runtime assumptions, and weak scale coverage.</div>
++      <div class="step"><span class="n">4</span><b>Harden the plan</b>Updated <code>BUILD_PLAN.md</code> so known gaps are treated as blocking work, not as solved problems.</div>
++      <div class="step"><span class="n">5</span><b>Prioritize fixes</b>Added a file-by-file prototype fix list to <code>PLAN_REVIEW.md</code> so the next implementation pass has a clear order.</div>
++    </div>
++  </div>
++
++  <div class="flow">
++    <div class="step"><span class="n">Hooks pass</span><b>Reduce wasted runtime</b>We then asked how hooks could speed up future runs. The answer was: use cheap, deterministic hooks to flag evaluator/comparator/generator risks before and after edits.</div>
++    <div class="step"><span class="n">Plan update</span><b>Add hook guidance</b>The plan was updated with a small table showing which hooks to add, when they fire, what they check, and why they matter for this repo.</div>
++    <div class="step"><span class="n">Export pass</span><b>Save the review record</b>Finally, we exported prompts, raw session files, and git history as text-only artifacts, then wrote this HTML summary.</div>
++  </div>
++
++  <h3>What changed in engineering terms</h3>
++  <ul>
++    <li><b>Before:</b> the plan was broadly correct, but it spoke too confidently about prototype evidence.</li>
++    <li><b>After:</b> the plan distinguishes prototype evidence from production-ready guarantees.</li>
++    <li><b>Before:</b> prototype limitations existed mostly as scattered notes.</li>
++    <li><b>After:</b> they are grouped, prioritized, and tied to concrete files and follow-up work.</li>

+++<h2 id="lessons">What we learned</h2>
+++<ol>
+++  <li><b>The big wins are generic.</b> Filter first, build strings late, gather only the columns that reach <code>OUT</code>, delete dead code, use TOPK. These gave 4–8.5× on q0001, q0004 and q0007. The self-join idioms win most on large data (20–47×), and they are the riskiest.</li>
+++  <li><b>Correctness may use constraints, never stats.</b> <code>customers</code> has no key, so assuming <code>c_id</code> is unique is a real bug, caught by the q0004 baseline.</li>
+++  <li><b>NULL semantics are the main trap.</b> HJOIN drops NULL keys but GROUP keeps them, and NULLIFE turns <code>''</code> into NULL.</li>
+++  <li><b>An operation may only run on a subset of the rows it originally ran on.</b> Removing work can only remove errors, which is allowed.</li>
+++  <li><b>Weak data hides bugs.</b> The example data passed two broken q0007 variants, and generated data missed a q0004 bug until literals from the programs were planted in it.</li>
+++  <li><b>Multiset comparison is too lenient</b> when the program sorts, and an order rule fixes it. <b>The output JSON has no types</b>, so BOOL must never equal INT, and only text in minivm's own number format may be compared as a number.</li>
+++  <li><b>Test the tester.</b> Zero defects proves nothing until seeded bugs are caught and honest-but-different optimizers pass.</li>
+++  <li><b>Measure the harness too.</b> The platform binary is 4.6× faster than the wrapper, which leaves the 2-minute budget roomy.</li>
+++</ol>

Each\n    11|line holds one instruction. A `;` starts a comment, which runs to the end of\n    12|the line; a line may hold only a comment, or be blank. Spaces and tabs are\n    13|interchangeable: they separate the opcode from its operands, and may indent a\n    14|line or surround an operand.\n    15|\n    16|```text\n    17|; Ids and amounts of orders over 100.\n    18|load   id, orders.o_id\n    19|load   amt, orders.o_amt\n    20|gt     m, amt, 100      ; NULL where o_amt is NULL\n    21|idx    i, m\n    22|gather a, id, i\n    23|gather b, amt, i\n    24|out    a, b\n    25|```\n    26|\n    27|The program must end with its only `OUT`; see [Program rules](running.md#program-rules).\n    28|\n    29|## Instructions\n    30|\n    31|An instruction is an opcode followed by comma-separated operands:\n    32|\n    33|```text\n    34|OP dest, operand, ...\n    35|```\n    36|\n    37|Opcodes are case-insensitive: `gt`, `Gt` and `GT` are the same instruction.\n    38|So are the keywords `NULL`, `TRUE`, `FALSE`, `ASC`, `DESC`, `NF`, `NL` and\n    39|`NULLEQ`.\n    40|Each opcode's operands are given on its page in the\n    41|[instruction reference](instructions/README.md).\n    42|\n    43|## Registers\n    44|\n    45|Register names are identifiers, such as `r1`, `amt` or `_t0`: a letter or `_`,\n    46|followed by letters, digits and `_`. Register names are case-sensitive, and a\n    47|keyword can't be a register name. A group set assigns each of its rows a group number; groups are numbered from 0 in order of first appearance. [`GROUP`](#group) and [`GALL`](#gall) produce a group set. [`GID`](#gid) returns a column with one value per row; the aggregates [`GFIRST`](#gfirst) through [`GMAX`](#gmin-gmax) return a column with one value per group, the value for group `k` at position `k`. page gives the rules every program must follow, what happens on an error,\n     6|how to run a program with `bin/minivm`, and the JSON format of the tables it\n     7|reads.\n     8|\n     9|## Program rules\n    10|\n    11|The last instruction must be the program's only [`OUT`](instructions/columns.md#out).\n    12|\n    13|| Limit | Value |\n    14||---|---|\n    15|| instructions per program | at most 20,000 |\n    16|| values held by one register | at most 4,000,000 (a join's output counts) |\n    17|| values held by all registers together | at most 64,000,000; a long string counts as several values (about 1 per 32 bytes) |\n    18|| work per run | roughly 300,000,000 [cycles](cycles.md); see below |\n    19|| rows per table | at most 10,000 |\n    20|| program file | at most 4 MiB |\n    21|| table-set file | at most 32 MiB and 2,000,000 JSON values |\n    22|\n    23|The work limit stops runaway programs. It counts a run's cycles, but `HJOIN`\n    24|and `GROUP` and copying long strings use it up faster than their cycles\n    25|suggest, so such programs stop somewhat sooner. Exceeding it, like any other\n    26|limit, is an error. It has no effect on the cycles reported for a run that\n    27|finishes.\n    28|\n    29|## Errors\n    30|\n    31|Any error stops the program. No result is printed; the error goes to stderr\n    32|and `bin/minivm` exits with status 1.\n    33|\n    34|## Command line\n    35|\n    36|```sh\n    37|bin/minivm PROGRAM.mini TABLES.json\n    38|bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json\n    39|```\n    40|\n    41|runs the program in `PROGRAM.mini` on the [table set](#table-sets) in\n    42|`TABLES.json`. On success it prints one line of JSON to stdout and exits 0:\n    43|\n    44|```json\n    45|{\"ncols\": N, \"rows\": [...], \"cycles\": C}\n    46|```\n    47|\n    48|- `ncols` is the number of `OUT` operands.\n    49|- `rows` is the result, one array of `ncols` values per row.\n    50|  `NULL` is `null` and a BOOL is `true` or `false`. An INT is a JSON integer,\n    51|  or a string of its digits outside -2^63 .. 2^63-1. A NUM is a string that keeps\n    52|  its digits after the point (`\"250.00\"`), a STR a string, and a DATE a string\n    53|  `\"YYYY-MM-DD\"`.\n    54|- `cycles` is the program's cost ([Cycles](cycles.md)).\n    55|\n    56|| Exit status | Meaning |\n    57||---|---|\n    58|| 0 | success; the result is on stdout |\n    59|| 1 | error; the message is on stderr |\n    60|| 2 | wrong number of arguments; a usage line is on stderr |\n    61|\n    62|With the program from [Language](language.md#programs) saved as\n    63|`over100.mini` and the [example table set](#example) as `orders.json`:\n    64|\n    65|```sh\n    66|$ bin/minivm over100.mini orders.json\n    67|{\"ncols\":2,\"rows\":[[1,\"250.00\"]],\"cycles\":42}\n    68|```\n    69|\n    70|`bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json` prints the table set's [schema file](#schema-files)\n    71|as one line of JSON instead of running a program.\n    72|\n    73|A program that compares a DATE with an INT stops with an error:\n    74|\n    75|```text\n    76|LOAD d, orders.o_date\n    77|GT   m, d, 5\n    78|OUT  m\n    79|```\n    80|\n    81|```sh\n    82|$ bin/minivm bad.mini orders.json\n    83|error: line 2: GT: expected a number, got DATE\n    84|```\n    85|\n    86|## Table sets\n    87|\n    88|A table set is a JSON object mapping each table name to its columns and rows:\n    89|\n    90|```json\n    91|{\"<table>\": {\"columns\": [{\"name\": \"c\", \"type\": \"INT|NUM|STR|DATE\"}], \"rows\": [[...], ...]}}\n    92|```\n    93|\n    94|- Table and column names are identifiers (letters, digits and `_`, not starting\n    95|  with a digit), compared without regard to case. Duplicate names are an error.\n    96|- `columns` lists each column's `name` and `type`, one of `INT`, `NUM`, `STR`, `DATE`.\n    97|- `rows` lists each row as an array of values, one per column, in column order.\n    98|  A table without `rows` is empty.\n    99|- A table may also declare [constraints](#constraints).\n   100|- Any key other than those shown or listed there is an error, as is a repeated key.\n   101|- A table holds at most 10,000 rows.\n   102|- INT values are JSON integers that fit in 32 bits.\n   103|- NUM values may be JSON numbers or strings. They must be exact, in the\n   104|  [NUM range](values.md#num-range).\n   105|- Dates are strings `\"YYYY-MM-DD\"`, years 0001 to 9999.\n   106|- JSON `null` is `NULL`.\n   107|\n   108|A program reads a stored column with `LOAD d, table.column` ([`LOAD`](instructions/columns.md#load)).\n   109|\n   110|### Constraints\n   111|\n   112|A table may declare what its rows guarantee. `bin/minivm` checks every declared\n   113|constraint when it reads the table set, and a table set that breaks one is an error.\n   114|\n   115|| Key | Example | Guarantee |\n   116||---|---|---|\n   117|| `key` | `[\"l_order\", \"l_no\"]` | the columns are never `NULL`, and no two rows agree on all of them |\n   118|| `not_null` | `[\"p_price\"]` | the columns are never `NULL` |\n   119|| `refs` | `{\"l_prod\": \"products.p_id\"}` | every non-NULL value of the column is a value of the other column, which must be its table's whole `key` and have the same type (INT and NUM may refer to each other) |\n   120|| `check` | `{\"l_qty\": [1, 500]}` | every non-NULL value lies between the bounds, inclusive; `null` leaves a side open; INT, NUM and DATE columns only |\n   121|| `sorted` | `[\"l_order\", \"l_no\"]` | the rows are stored in ascending order of the columns, as `ASC NF` sorts them |\n   122|\n   123|Values are compared as in [Ordering](values.md#ordering), so NUM keys `1.0` and\n   124|`1.00` are the same key. Column names in constraints are compared without regard\n   125|to case, and naming a column twice in one constraint is an error. A pair is SKIPPED if the original errors. It is a DEFECT if the optimizer fails or takes more than 1 s, if the optimized program errors, if ncols differ, or if the rows differ. Rows are compared in order when the original specifies order (SORT/TOPK reaching OUT), otherwise as a multiset. Numbers match within 1e-6 relative. Larger datasets speed up much more, because the originals' quadratic self-joins grow with the data.\n\n  | Program | q0001 | q0002 | q0003 | q0004 | q0005 | q0006 | q0007 | q0008 |\n  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n  | Speedup on example data | 8.1× | 1.8× | 3.0× | 8.5× | 1.7× | 3.0× | 4.1× | 1.2× |\n  | Speedup on large data | 4.5× | 1.8× | 37× | 47× | 2.2× | 20× | 8.3× | 1.3× |\n\n- **Correctness:** all 8 hand-optimized programs match the originals on all 40 datasets, and all 8 naive baselines are caught.\n- **Evaluator:** catches 11 of 11 buggy fakes with 0 false alarms on 8 honest ones. A full run takes 1.7 s.\n\n## What we learned\n1. **The biggest wins are generic, not clever.** Filter before joining and before building strings. Gather only the columns that reach `OUT`. Delete dead code. Use TOPK instead of SORT followed by a slice. These gave most of q0001, q0004 and q0007 (4–8.5×). Replacing a self-join with GROUP is the only big structural rewrite (q0003, q0006), and it is also the riskiest.\n2. **Rewrites must rely on constraints, never on stats.**\n   - Exactly one match is safe for `not_null` + `refs` to a key.\n   - A SORT is a no-op on a `sorted` table.\n   - `customers` has no key, so a join to it can multiply rows. The naive q0004, which assumes unique `c_id`, is wrong on data where `c_id` repeats.\n3. **NULL semantics are the main trap.** HJOIN never matches NULL keys, but GROUP puts NULLs together. NULLIFE turns `''` into NULL. IS is never NULL. Every self-join→GROUP rewrite needs an explicit NULL-key filter.\n4. **Safety rule for rewrites:** an operation may only run on a *subset* of the rows it originally ran on. Removing work can only remove errors, which is allowed because \"if the input program errors, anything goes\".\n5. **Weak data hides bugs.**\n   - Two broken q0007 variants (TOPK 4 instead of 5, flipped tie-break) passed the example data. It has only 3 July-2023 orders and no tied amounts.\n   - The q0004 naive baseline went uncaught until the generator planted the programs' own literals: no category was ever `'KITCHEN'`, so every result was empty.\n   - Fix: harvest literals and their ±1 neighbours, and generate more rows than every TOPK limit, plus ties.\n6. **Multiset comparison alone is too lenient.** It missed a reversed-rows bug and barely caught sort-key bugs (4 and 2 defects). The order rule raised these to 172, 134 and 19 defects with no new false alarms.\n7. **The output JSON has no types.**\n   - STR `\"2.00\"` prints like a NUM.\n   - Only text minivm actually prints as a number (`-?\\d+(\\.\\d+)?`) may be compared numerically; otherwise a TRIM bug on `'1.0 '` would hide.\n   - JSON `true` must never equal `1`.\n   - Remaining ambiguity: STR `'1.0'` vs `'1.00'`.\n8. **Test the tester, and test it with evidence.** An evaluator that reports 0 defects proves nothing until it has caught seeded bugs and passed honest-but-different optimizers. Honest examples include renaming registers, INT→NUM scale changes, and 1e-10 drift.\n9. **Calling the platform binary directly is 4.6× faster than the `bin/minivm` wrapper** (8.3 ms vs 38.6 ms per run, identical output). This leaves the 2-minute evaluator budget roomy: about 14k VM runs in 2 minutes on 16 cores, even before parallel overhead.\n\n## Known gaps (next steps for the real build)\n- **Programs:** only the 8 example programs are tested. Binaries in history (BUILD_PLAN §11) are still an open item.\n    30|- **Budget overrun:** a full eval with 3 seeds and the meta-eval on every small edit burns both wall time and tokens.\n    31|\n    32|## Recommendations\n    33|**Roles and context (who sees what)**\n    34|- *Orchestrator* (main session): owns BUILD_PLAN, writes one **task card** per iteration (`notes/tasks/NN.md`: goal, rewrite rank, safety rule, done-definition). It doesn't write optimizer code.\n    35|- *Builder* subagent: gets the task card, `optimizer/`, docs. Requirements: how we meet each one, and how we prove it\n\n| # | Requirement (one-pager) | How we meet it | Proof |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| R1 | `./optimize program.mini schema.json` prints a program | Python 3 stdlib. On any internal error, or an estimate that isn't cheaper, it prints the input unchanged | runner: exit 0, `bin/minivm` parses the output |\n| R2 | Same results on any data satisfying the schema's constraints | rewrites justified only by semantics and **constraints** (never stats); safety rules in §5 | evaluator over generated data, plus meta-eval |\n| R3 | Order doesn't matter unless the program specifies it | the optimizer always preserves order; the evaluator compares in order when the original specifies it (§4.3) | `b_reverse` caught (172 defects) **[M]** |\n| R4 | Numbers within 1e-6 relative | the optimizer doesn't change arithmetic; the comparator compares Decimal values with relative tolerance | `h_tiny_drift` OK, `b_drift` caught **[M]** |\n| R5 | If the input program errors, anything goes | the evaluator skips pairs where the original errors | rubric O5 |\n| R6 | ≤ 1 s per program | linear passes; internal deadline at 0.8 s, then fall back | runner reports max optimizer time |\n| R7 | Noticeably faster, on unseen programs and data | general passes (§3), held-out generated programs | perf report: geomean speedup on examples and on held-out programs |\n| R8 | `./evaluate OPTIMIZER` exits 0 or non-zero; works for any optimizer with the same CLI | black box: subprocess call plus `bin/minivm` only | meta-eval verdict table |\n| R9 | Evaluator ≤ 2 min, may use `bin/minivm` | platform binary (8.3 ms/run), parallel, watchdog at 100 s | wall time in every report |\n| R10 | Submission: code, prompts, logs, raw sessions, git history, no binaries, models and spend, \"few days\" plan | §11 | checklist |\n\n---\n\n## 2. What the examples were hiding (learnings from hand-optimizing)\n\nEach row: the original program's cost, what made it slow, and what that means for the optimizer.\n\n| Example | Cycles orig → hand **[M]** | Hidden lesson |\n|---|---|---|\n| q0001 | 13766 → 1703 (8.1×) | 52% of the cycles are CAT and LEFT building a label for rows a later filter throws away. **Order of work matters more than the work itself.** `SORT` on `lines` is a no-op because of the `sorted` constraint. `GE l_qty,1` is always TRUE because of `not_null` + `check`. |\n| q0002 | 3617 → 2011 (1.8×) | The self-join's *counted* side must stay unfiltered. Filtering it too is the naive bug (`q0002.naive`, caught on 17 datasets). Only the outer side may shrink. |\n| q0003 | 8562 → 2817 (3.0×; 37× on large) | A \"count of better rows\" self-join is O(n²) per group. A sort plus per-group rank is linear. The HJOIN silently drops NULL and `''`→NULL keys, and the rewrite must reproduce that. |\n| q0004 | 18442 → 2179 (8.5×; 47× on large) | 36% of the cycles are GATHER fan-out across 4 joins. A SORT before GALL/GSUM is useless. **`customers` has no key**, so de-duplicating `c_id` is wrong (`q0004.naive`). |\n| q0005 | 5518 → 3294 (1.7×) | Join, then sort, then GROUP de-dup is really a **semi-join**. De-duplicate the small side first. |\n| q0006 | 6338 → 2091 (3.0×; 20× on large) | A self-join followed by GMAX is GROUP + GMAX + GID. GROUP puts NULLs in one group but HJOIN never matches them, so an explicit NULL filter is required (`q0006.naive`). |\n| q0007 | 2596 → 637 (4.1×) | Filter first, then TOPK instead of SORT, then build the label for 5 rows. The example data has only 3 July-2023 orders and no tied amounts, so `TOPK 4` and a flipped tie-break both **passed on the example data**. |\n| q0008 | 1524 → 1249 (1.2×) | Already tight. Dead loads are the only waste. Not every legacy program is slow. |\n\n**Cross-cutting.**\n1. The biggest wins are generic, and the clever rewrites are the riskiest:\n   - The generic wins are filter-first, late materialization, GATHER sinking, dead-code elimination, and TOPK instead of SORT.\n   - The self-join idioms give the largest gains on large data, and they are also the riskiest.\n2. Constraints carry the correctness argument:\n   - `not_null` + `refs` to a `key` means exactly one match.\n   - `sorted` means a SORT on those keys is a no-op.\n   - A table with **no key** can fan out a join.\n3. **Weak data hides bugs.**\n   - A q0004 baseline was missed until the generator planted the programs' own literals (`'KITCHEN'`).\n   - Every gain is relative to the data: on small datasets speedups shrink to 1.2–3× because the filter results are often empty.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Optimizer design\n\n**Pipeline.**\n1. Parse into an SSA IR.\n2. Annotate each register: source table, row domain, type, nullability, sortedness, ordered/monotone.\n3. Run the passes to a fixpoint.\n4. Estimate cost with the `[doc: cycles.md#cost-table]` model.\n5. Emit.\n\n**Global guard:** if the estimated cost isn't lower, an intermediate result would grow, or any pass throws an exception, emit the input unchanged.\n\n| Rank | Rewrite | Gain | Risk | Safety rule (§5) | Prototype evidence |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | Dead-code elimination + CSE | 5–25% | very low | S1 | `h_dce` honest, 0 false alarms |\n| 2 | GATHER composition / sinking; gather only the columns that reach OUT | 20–50% on wide plans | low | S7 | q0001, q0004 |\n| 3 | Filter first; run element-wise ops after filters (late materialization) | 4–8× on q0001/q0004/q0007 | low | S2, S6 | q0007 2596→637 **[M]** |\n| 4 | Sort reduction: TOPK for SORT+slice, dead SORT before order-insensitive aggregates, SORT on `sorted` keys is identity | 5–20% | med | S4, S5 | q0001, q0004, q0007 |\n| 5 | Filter pushdown below joins (one-sided, total predicates) | 30–70% on q0004-like plans | med | S2, S3 | q0004 |\n| 6 | Constraint rewrites: always-TRUE predicates, exactly-one-match joins | small | med | S8 | q0001 |\n| 7 | Join algorithm choice (HJOIN↔NLJOIN by cost; stats allowed here) | small | very low | — | `h_join_swap` honest; NLJOIN is cheaper when one side has ≤ ~5 rows |\n| 8 | Idioms: self-join+aggregate → GROUP; rank via sort; semi-join de-dup | 2–47× | **high** | S3, S4, S9 | q0003, q0005, q0006 |\n\n**Skip entirely:** arithmetic re-association, join reordering, anything that uses stats for correctness.\n**Gate:** rank 8 is enabled only after 0 defects on NULL-, tie-, scale- and empty-table-heavy data.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Evaluator design (`./evaluate OPTIMIZER`)\n\n1. **Corpus.**\n   - Programs: the 8 examples, mutants of the examples, and generated programs from a type-checked template generator over the schema (scan/filter, 1–4 joins along `refs`, GROUP aggregates, SORT/TOPK/SLICE, string/date/arithmetic) with legacy bloat added. Keep a program only if the original succeeds and gives non-empty output on at least one dataset.\n   - Data: `gen_data.py` style, constraint-respecting, adversarial, with literals harvested from the programs, all validated by `--schema`. Plus datasets designed to make originals error.\n2. **Run.** One optimizer call per program, at most 4 in parallel so machine load can't cause a false \"> 1 s\". Then VM runs on all cores using the platform binary.\n3. **Compare** using the rubric in §6.\n   - Order: a data-flow pass over the original decides whether output order is specified (`eval-proto.py: output_ordered`).\n   - Ties: compare rows tied on the sort keys as a multiset, by running an *instrumented* original that also outputs the sort keys (still to build).\n4. **On a defect:** re-run once, save the repro (program, optimized program, dataset, diff) to `eval_out/`, then shrink it if time remains (stretch goal). Exit 1.\n5. **Budget [M]:** 8.3 ms per run means 320 checks take 1.7 s. A watchdog at 100 s stops new work and reports the verdict so far.\n\n### 4.1 Evaluation methods compared\n\n| Method | How | Proves | Catches | False-alarm risk | Cost within 2 min | Use |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **Run-and-compare (differential testing)** | run original and optimized on many datasets, compare outputs | that a defect exists (a counterexample); never that there is none | anything the data exercises: NULLs, ties, order, errors, scale | low, if the comparator rules are right | ~1.7 s per 320 checks **[M]** | **primary** |\n| **Normalize-and-compare (syntactic)** | canonicalize both programs (rename registers, DCE, sort commutative ops) and diff them | equivalence only when they normalize to identical text | nothing, if any real rewrite happened | none, but almost always \"unknown\" | ms | fast path: identical after normalizing ⇒ skip running the VM |\n| **Metamorphic testing (SQLancer TLP/NoREC, EMI)** | derive related programs or data, e.g. partition on `p` / `NOT p` / `p IS NULL`, add dead code, permute rows that are unsorted by the program | defects that need no reference output | NULL three-valued-logic bugs, order assumptions, stats-as-constraint bugs | low | moderate | data-side only: NULL partitions and row permutations in the generator |\n| **Property checks** | invariants without a reference: `ncols` same, row count same for pure projections, VM limits, optimizer time | gross failures | crashes, timeouts, limit blow-ups | none | trivial | always on |\n| **Mutation testing of the oracle** | seed bugs into fake optimizers; measure the kill rate | the *evaluator's* recall and precision | weak data, a lenient comparator | — | ~37 s for 19 fakes **[M]** | meta-eval gate on every evaluator change |\n| **Translation validation / math proof (Alive2, CompCert)** | encode both programs symbolically under the constraints and ask an SMT solver whether they are equivalent | **equivalence on all data** | everything, within the encoded semantics | none, if the encoding is right | days to build; may be slow per query; semantics are large (NUM rounding, Unicode UPPER, 3-valued logic) | out of scope for 2–3 h; first item in the \"few days\" plan |\n| **Bounded exhaustive (small-scope hypothesis)** | enumerate all tiny databases (e.g. ≤ 3 rows, small value domains) | equivalence on every database up to that size | most semantic bugs, which show up on tiny data | none | grows exponentially with columns and values; feasible for 1–2 tables | stretch goal: NULL/''/tie value domains on 0–3 rows |\n\n**Decision:** run-and-compare is the verdict. Normalize-and-compare is a fast path. Metamorphic ideas shape the data generator. Mutation testing gates the evaluator. Proofs are deferred.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Safety rules: how a rewrite can produce wrong output (with doc citations)\n\n| ID | Trap | Doc evidence | Probe **[M]** | Rule |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| S1 | **Adding an error.** Errors stop the program, and an optimized program that errors is a defect. Removing dead code can only remove errors, which is fine because \"if the input errors, anything goes\". | \"Any error stops the program\" `[doc: running.md#errors]`; dead `DIV x,0` still errors | F6, `b_dead_div0` caught (272) | Never add an op that may error. Deleting ops is always allowed. |\n| S2 | **Data-dependent errors.** Type errors and DIV by 0 fire only on rows actually used, never on empty or all-NULL columns. | \"Types are checked row by row ... whether a program fails can depend on its data\" `[doc: instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions]`; \"DIV of NULL by 0 is NULL\" (same section) | `DIV` after a `d≠0` filter OK, before it errors | An op may run only on a **subset** of the rows it originally ran on. Never push DIV/IDIV/MOD/DATEADD/overflow-prone ops or comparisons of mixed types above a filter. |\n| S3 | **NULL keys: joins vs groups.** HJOIN never matches NULL keys (unless NULLEQ); GROUP puts NULLs together. | \"A NULL key matches no key, unless ... NULLEQ\" `[doc: instructions/joins.md]`; \"NULL equals NULL\" `[doc: instructions/grouping.md#group]` | `q0006.naive` caught (24), `b_nulleq` caught (56) | Any join↔group rewrite adds or keeps an explicit `NOT ISNULL(key)` filter. |\n| S4 | **Order and ties.** SORT is stable, HJOIN output is ordered by (i, j), and groups are numbered by first appearance. | \"Ties keep their input order\" `[doc: instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys]`; \"ordered by i then j\" `[doc: joins.md]`; \"groups are numbered from 0 in order of first appearance\" `[doc: grouping.md#group-sets]` | `b_reverse` (172), `b_no_tiebreak` (19) | Preserve exact output order. Never swap join sides or reorder the input to GROUP/GFIRST/GMIN/GMAX. |\n| S5 | **First-of-equals and NUM scale.** GMIN/GMAX return the first of equal values; GSUM uses the largest scale in the group; `1.0` and `1.00` print differently. | \"the first of equals: of 1, 1.0 and 1.00, whichever comes first\" `[doc: grouping.md#gmin-gmax]`; \"1.0 and 1.00 are equal but print differently\" `[doc: values.md#num-range]`; GSUM scale `[doc: grouping.md#gsum]` | F28, F5 | Keep the aggregate input order. Avoid identities that rescale (`x*1.000`, `x+0.0`): equal in value, but they change the printed text. |\n| S6 | **Unicode changes length.** UPPER can change the character count, so UPPER and LEFT/SUBSTR don't commute. | \"UPPER('straße') is 'STRASSE'\" `[doc: strings.md#upper]` | `ß` in generator | Never reorder string ops relative to each other; only move them across filters and gathers. |\n| S7 | **VM limits.** Join output counts toward limits; HJOIN/GROUP use up the work budget faster than their cycles suggest. | limits table `[doc: running.md#program-rules]` | 2M-row join takes 425 ms | No rewrite may grow any intermediate result beyond the original's. |\n| S8 | **Constraints vs stats.** Constraints hold for every dataset; stats describe one. `check` doesn't imply `not_null`. Tables without a `key` may have duplicates. | \"The constraints hold for every table set with this schema; the stats describe only this one\" `[doc: running.md#schema-files]`; constraint table `[doc: running.md#constraints]` | `q0004.naive` (no key on customers) | Correctness may use only key, not_null, refs, check and sorted. Stats are used only for cost. |\n| S9 | **`sorted` covers stored order only.** It survives IDX, ascending GATHER and the left side of a join, but not the right side of HJOIN, GROUP output, or a SORT on other keys. | \"the rows are stored in ascending order ... as ASC NF sorts them\" `[doc: running.md#constraints]` | q0001/q0005 identity SORT | Drop a SORT only if its keys are a prefix of `sorted` ASC NF *and* the index is proven ascending from LOAD. |\n| S10 | **Literal-only ops and OUT rules.** An element-wise op needs at least one register operand; OUT must be the last instruction and the only OUT. | `[doc: instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions]`, `[doc: running.md#program-rules]` | F23, F25 | Constant folding must not produce a literal-only op; the emitter always ends with exactly one OUT. |\n\n---\n\n## 6. Eval rubric\n\n```json\n{\n  \"outputs\": {\n    \"O1_ncols\": \"equal; optimized must succeed whenever original succeeds\",\n    \"O2_rows\": \"in order if original specifies order (SORT/TOPK reaches OUT), else multiset\",\n    \"O3_numbers\": \"JSON int or string matching ^-?\\\\d+(\\\\.\\\\d+)?$ -> Decimal, |a-b| <= 1e-6*max(|a|,|b|)\",\n    \"O4_other_values\": \"NULL==NULL only; STR/DATE exact (no Unicode normalization); BOOL never equals INT\",\n    \"O5_skip\": \"original errors -> pair skipped, not a defect\",\n    \"O6_limits\": \"optimizer > 1 s, crash, empty output, or optimized VM error -> defect\"\n  },\n  \"programs\": {\n    \"P1_cycles\": \"speedup per (program, dataset) + geomean\",\n    \"P2_instructions\": \"count before/after\",\n    \"P3_peak_register\": \"never larger than original\",\n    \"P4_optimizer_time_max_s\": \"< 1.0\",\n    \"P5_regressions\": \"optimized cycles > original on any dataset (reported, target 0)\"\n  },\n  \"evaluator\": {\n    \"E1_recall\": \"caught / buggy fakes (seeded + held-out), target 100%\",\n    \"E2_false_alarms\": \"flagged honest fakes, target 0 over 10 seeds\",\n    \"E3_wall_time_s\": \"< 120 (target < 60 at -j4)\",\n    \"E4_determinism\": \"same seed -> identical report\"\n  }\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n## 7. Unclear rules and the assumptions we make\n\nHow we handle each: pick the **default that can't produce a false alarm or a wrong optimization**, encode it as a check, log it, and escalate only if the choice changes more than 20% of results.\n\n| # | Unclear point | Options | Default | Why | Encoded in |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Q1 | When does a program \"specify\" order? Do tied rows count? | (a) whenever SORT/TOPK reaches OUT, strict; (b) the same, but tied rows compared as a multiset; (c) never | **(b)**; today (a) | strict order flags legal reorders of ties | `output_ordered`; tie handling still to build |\n| Q2 | `\"2.0\"` vs `\"2.00\"`; INT `2` vs NUM `\"2.0\"` | text equal / numeric equal | numeric equal | \"numbers within 1e-6\" | `tricky_checks.py` CMP |\n| Q3 | STR `'1.0'` vs `'1.00'` print like numbers | infer column types / treat as numbers | treat as numbers (documented gap) | the output JSON has no types | known gap; fix by inferring types |\n| Q4 | Tolerance on INTs (`10000000` vs `10000001` passes) | apply to INTs / exact for INTs | apply (spec says \"numbers\") | follow the spec literally | CMP check |\n| Q5 | Near zero (`0` vs `1e-7`) | relative only / add an absolute epsilon | relative only | spec says relative; correct optimizers don't change arithmetic | CMP check |\n| Q6 | Ties at a TOPK/SLICE/GFIRST cut-off | fail / warn | warn once tie handling is built | a correct optimizer may choose another tied row | still to build |\n| Q7 | Optimizer may use `bin/minivm`? | yes / no | no | the grader may not ship it next to `./optimize` | optimizer design |\n| Q8 | Can stats be used? | correctness / cost only | cost only | `[doc: running.md#schema-files]` | S8 |\n| Q9 | Optimized program hits a VM limit where the original didn't | defect / skip | defect | the program \"gives a different result\" (none) | O6 |\n| Q10 | How is \"faster\" measured? | cycles / wall time | cycles | that's what the VM reports | P1 |\n\n---\n\n## 8. Working model: how the agents talk\n\n**Roles.**\n- **Orchestrator** (main session): owns the plan and writes task cards; never writes optimizer code.\n- **Builder** subagent: implements one rewrite per task.\n- **Red-team** subagent: sees only the spec, docs and rubric. It writes fake optimizers and adversarial data, and never sees the optimizer code.\n- **Checker:** the `./evaluate` script, not an LLM.\n- **Reviewer** subagent: fresh context, for rank ≥ 5 rewrites. Its job: \"name the dataset that breaks this\".\n- **Human:** approves at checkpoints and decides open questions.\n\n```\nhuman ──approve/decide──▶ ORCHESTRATOR ──task.json──▶ BUILDER ──commit + build.json──▶ CHECKER(./evaluate)\n  ▲                          │  ▲                                                        │\n  └────escalation.json───────┘  └──────verdict.json ◀── REVIEWER ◀── report.json ◀──────┘\n                                 RED-TEAM (spec only) ──fakes + data──▶ CHECKER (meta-eval)\n```\n\n**Rules.**\n- Agents communicate only through **files**, never prose summaries.\n- Every message is a JSON document with a schema version.\n- Prose goes only in a `notes` field.\n- Files live under `runs/<iteration>/`.\n\n```json\n// task.json  (orchestrator -> builder)\n{\"v\":1,\"task_id\":\"T07\",\"goal\":\"sort reduction: SORT+IDX+SLICE -> IDX+TOPK\",\n \"rewrite_rank\":4,\"safety_rules\":[\"S4\",\"S5\"],\"files_allowed\":[\"optimizer/passes/sort.py\",\"tests/cases/medium/*\"],\n \"done_when\":{\"defects\":0,\"geomean_min\":1.0,\"opt_time_max_s\":0.8},\"budget\":{\"wall_min\":15,\"tokens_k\":200}}\n```\n```json\n// build.json  (builder -> checker)\n{\"v\":1,\"task_id\":\"T07\",\"commit\":\"abc1234\",\"pass\":\"sort_reduction\",\"tests_added\":[\"medium/topk_after_filter.mini\"],\n \"claims\":[{\"rule\":\"S4\",\"why\":\"TOPK = first n of the same stable SORT [doc: sorting.md#topk]\"}],\"notes\":\"\"}\n```\n```json\n// report.json  (checker -> everyone; also appended to notes/runs.jsonl)\n{\"v\":1,\"commit\":\"abc1234\",\"seed\":0,\"checked\":320,\"skipped\":0,\"defects\":0,\"wall_s\":1.7,\n \"geomean_speedup\":2.39,\"per_program\":[{\"name\":\"q0007\",\"speedup\":4.08,\"status\":\"OK\"}],\n \"meta\":{\"buggy_caught\":11,\"buggy_total\":11,\"false_alarms\":0},\n \"defect_repros\":[]}\n```\n```json\n// verdict.json  (reviewer -> orchestrator)\n{\"v\":1,\"commit\":\"abc1234\",\"decision\":\"keep|revert|needs_test\",\n \"counterexample\":{\"program\":\"...\",\"dataset\":\"...\",\"expected\":\"...\",\"got\":\"...\"},\"rules_checked\":[\"S4\"]}\n```\n```json\n// escalation.json  (orchestrator -> human)\n{\"v\":1,\"question_id\":\"Q1\",\"options\":[\"strict\",\"tie-multiset\"],\"recommended\":\"tie-multiset\",\n \"impact\":\"3/320 checks change verdict\",\"blocking\":true}\n```\n\n**Git discipline.**\n- One rewrite per commit.\n- A red build gets `git revert`, never a reset or amend.\n- Tag green checkpoints `cp1`…`cp5`.\n- Each defect becomes a regression in `tests/regressions/`, replayed first on every run.\n\n**Independence.** `evaluate/` never imports `optimizer/`; a grep check enforces this. Only the CLI and `bin/minivm` cross the boundary.\n\n---\n\n## 9. Stopping criteria\n\n```json\n{\n  \"success\": [\"0 defects on 3 seeds\", \"meta-eval: 100% buggy caught (seeded + held-out), 0 false alarms\",\n              \"geomean >= 2x on examples, > 1x on held-out programs\", \"max optimizer time < 1 s\", \"evaluate < 60 s\"],\n  \"no_more_improvement\": \"2 consecutive iterations with < 3% geomean gain -> move to next rank or stop\",\n  \"budget\": \"user time 2h45m or token cap reached -> ship last green tag\",\n  \"ask_human\": [\"a rule depends on Q1-Q10\", \"a defect not explained in 2 attempts\",\n                \"a fix would drop > 20% of the gain\", \"any destructive git action\"],\n  \"hard_rule\": \"any defect = red build; revert or disable the rewrite before anything else\"\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n## 10. (The template below is section-level only because each source is section-specific.)\n- Keep it machine-readable: list every query / table / file each part draws on, plus any parameters or assumptions a future update needs.\n- **Record every query as `{ \"type\": \"query\", \"sql\": \"<the SQL text>\" }` in a `dataSources` array** — the SQL itself, never under another key (such as `query` or `originalQuery`) and never as a path to a `.sql` file. That includes the query that produced a file you were given: add a `query` source with the SQL copied in, alongside a `{ \"type\": \"file\", \"path\": \"…\" }` source for the file. Keeping every query in the same place and shape lets a later run, or a script, find them all.\n- Update it whenever you change what the report shows.\n- Tokens in `{…}` (e.g. `{DATABASE}.{SCHEMA}.{TABLE}`) are placeholders — replace them with the report's real fully-qualified sources.\n- Include only fields you know. `\"warehouse\"` is optional: record it when a warehouse was actually used or named, and delete the field when none was. Omit any other field whose value you don't have too. Never leave a `{…}` token in the saved file.\n\n---\n\n## What you can and can't use\n\n**Use freely:**\n- ✅ Inline `<script>` — put all your JavaScript here.\n- ✅ Inline `<style>` and `style=\"…\"` attributes.\n- ✅ `<canvas>`, inline `<svg>`, and the vendored `/libs/` libraries (below).\n- ✅ Images as `data:` or `blob:` URIs.\n\n**Don't use** (silently dropped or blocked):\n- ❌ Inline event handlers (`onclick=`, `onload=`, …) — attach handlers with `addEventListener` inside a `<script>`.\n- ❌ `eval`, `new Function`, or `setTimeout(\"…code…\")`.\n- ❌ External / CDN scripts, stylesheets, or web fonts — load only from `/libs/`.\n- ❌ Remote images (`<img src=\"https://…\">`) — inline the bytes as a `data:` URI.\n- ❌ Runtime network calls — `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `sendBeacon`. Embed all data directly in the HTML.\n- ❌ Cookies, `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` — unavailable in the sandbox.\n- ❌ `<iframe>`, `<object>`/`<embed>`, `<video>`/`<audio>`, Web Workers, `<form>` submission, `<base>`.\n\n---\n\n## Available libraries\n\nReference a vendored library by its **pinned path** — nothing else loads:\n\n```html\n<script src=\"/libs/chart.js@4.4.4/chart.umd.js\"></script>\n<link rel=\"stylesheet\" href=\"/libs/katex@0.16.21/katex.min.css\">\n```\n\n| Library | Reference path | Use / limits |\n|---|---|---|\n| chart.js | `/libs/chart.js@4.4.4/chart.umd.js` | Charts (renders to `<canvas>`) |\n| plotly (cartesian) | `/libs/plotly.js-cartesian-dist-min@2.35.2/plotly-cartesian.min.js` | Cartesian charts only |\n| d3 | `/libs/d3@7.9.0/d3.min.js` | Low-level data viz |\n| vega | `/libs/vega@6.2.0/vega.min.js` | Base for vega-lite / vega-embed |\n| vega-lite | `/libs/vega-lite@6.4.3/vega-lite.min.js` | Declarative charts |\n| vega-embed | `/libs/vega-embed@7.1.0/vega-embed.min.js` | Embeds a spec — **must** pass `{ ast: true }` |\n| mermaid | `/libs/mermaid@10.9.6/mermaid.min.js` | Diagrams (flowchart, sequence, class, state, ER, gantt, pie, gitGraph, journey, …) — **must init with `securityLevel: 'strict'`** |\n| katex | `/libs/katex@0.16.21/katex.min.js` + `/libs/katex@0.16.21/katex.min.css` | Math typesetting |\n| highlight.js | `/libs/highlight.js@11.10.0/highlight.min.js` + `/libs/highlight.js@11.10.0/github.min.css` | Code highlighting |\n| marked | `/libs/marked@14.1.3/marked.min.js` | Markdown → HTML |\n| three | `/libs/three@0.169.0/three.module.min.js` | 3D (WebGL); ES module |\n\nNotes:\n- **Mermaid:** initialize with `securityLevel: 'strict'` (required — it sanitizes diagram labels; never use `'loose'`). Images in labels must be `data:` URIs or inline `<svg>` — remote image URLs are blocked and won't load.\n- **Vega:** always pass `{ ast: true }` to `vegaEmbed` (required — without it the chart won't render). Give the spec an explicit numeric `width` (e.g. `width: 700`) — `width: 'container'` renders a zero-width, blank chart in the sandbox.\n- **KaTeX:** include both the JS and the CSS.\n- **three.js** is an ES module — load it with `<script type=\"module\">`.\n\n---\n\n## Theming (light & dark)\n\nReports adapt to the viewer's light or dark color scheme, so **make your CSS adapt too** — don't hard-code a light background with dark text (or vice-versa).\n\n- Use the `light-dark()` function for colors, e.g. `color: light-dark(#1f2937, #e5e7eb);`, and declare `:root { color-scheme: light dark; }`.\n- Or provide `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { … }` overrides.\n\n---\n\n## Responsive layout\n\nReports are opened on phones and in narrow side-panels as often as full-width, so the layout must **reflow, not overflow** — nothing should force horizontal page scrolling or spill past the viewport edge on a ~360px-wide screen. The `<meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width, initial-scale=1\">` tag (in the template) is what makes this possible — always keep it.\n\n- **Fluid container:** cap the width but let it shrink — `max-width: 880px; width: 100%; box-sizing: border-box;` — and use fluid padding like `padding: clamp(16px, 4vw, 24px);` so narrow screens aren't cramped and wide ones aren't sparse.\n- **Wide tables:** wrap every table in a horizontally scrollable container so the table scrolls on its own instead of stretching the whole page:\n  ```html\n  <div style=\"overflow-x: auto;\"><table>…</table></div>\n  ```\n- **Images & SVG:** add `img, svg { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }` so they never exceed the viewport width.\n- **Charts (chart.js):** wrap the `<canvas>` in a **fixed-height box** and let the chart fill it — put the height in CSS, never let the chart's own aspect ratio decide it. A ratio that looks right on desktop (e.g. a `1040×360` canvas, or `aspectRatio`/`height:auto` derived from it) collapses to a short unreadable sliver at phone width. See the pattern below (`.chart-box` + `responsive: true, maintainAspectRatio: false`). For Vega-Lite, `width: 'container'` renders blank in the sandbox, so keep a numeric `width` and wrap the chart in `<div style=\"overflow-x: auto;\">` so it scrolls when the screen is narrower than the chart.\n- **Charts (Plotly):** Plotly renders to a `<div>`, so the `.chart-box`/canvas pattern doesn't apply. Wrap it in a `width: 100%` container, set `layout: { autosize: true }` (no fixed `width`), and pass `{ responsive: true }` as the config to `Plotly.newPlot(...)` so it re-fits when the viewport changes.\n- **Avoid fixed pixel widths** on layout elements — prefer `%`, `max-width`, and `min()`/`clamp()`. For multi-column layouts use a grid/flex that collapses on narrow screens, e.g. `display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr));` or `display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap;`.\n- **Test narrow:** picture the report at ~360px wide — if anything is cut off or triggers horizontal scrolling of the whole page, constrain or wrap it.\n\n---\n\n## External links\n\nWrite normal links with real URLs:\n\n```html\n<a href=\"https://docs.snowflake.com/\">Docs</a>\n```\n\n- Hrefs with embedded userinfo (`https://user@host/…`) or a protocol-relative form (`//host/…`) are made inert — the text stays, but they aren't clickable.\n- `mailto:` and `tel:` links are kept as-is — use them for contact links.\n- Don't use `javascript:` or `data:` hrefs (they're stripped), and don't rely on JavaScript (`window.open`, `location = …`) to navigate.\n\n---\n\n## Charts & interactivity — the pattern\n\nPut all logic in an inline `<script>` and load the library from `/libs/`.\n\n**chart.js** — wrap the `<canvas>` in a fixed-height box and let the chart fill it. The box's CSS height controls the chart height at every screen width; `maintainAspectRatio: false` lets it span the full width:\n\n```html\n<style>\n  .chart-box { position: relative; width: 100%; height: 320px; }   /* height lives here */\n  .chart-box > canvas { width: 100% !important; height: 100% !important; }\n</style>\n<div class=\"chart-box\"><canvas id=\"rev\"></canvas></div>    <!-- no width/height attrs on the canvas -->\n<script src=\"/libs/chart.js@4.4.4/chart.umd.js\"></script>\n<script>\n  new Chart(document.getElementById('rev'), {\n    type: 'bar',\n    data: {\n      labels: ['North America', 'EMEA', 'APAC'],\n      datasets: [{ label: 'Revenue ($M)', data: [1.2, 0.5, 0.4] }],\n    },\n    options: { responsive: true, maintainAspectRatio: false },   // fill the box\n  });\n</script>\n```\n\n> This is the sizing that survives a narrow screen. **Don't** size a chart by its canvas `width`/`height` attributes or by `aspectRatio`/`height: auto` — a wide desktop ratio (e.g. `1040×360`) collapses to a ~100px-tall sliver at phone width. It runs straight-line programs whose\ninstructions each operate on whole columns of values, and it reports how many\ncycles each run costs.\n\n## Example\n\n```text\nLOAD    a, orders.o_amt\nGT      m, a, 100.00\nIDX     i, m\nGATHER  big, a, i\nOUT     big\n```\n\n- `LOAD` reads the stored column `orders.o_amt` into register `a`.\n- `GT` sets `m` to a BOOL column: `a > 100.00` at each row.\n- `IDX` sets `i` to the positions where `m` is TRUE.\n- `GATHER` sets `big` to the values of `a` at the positions in `i`.\n- `OUT` makes `big` the program's result.\n\nSaved as `big.mini`, run it from the bundle root:\n\n```sh\nbin/minivm big.mini examples/data.json\n```\n\nwhich prints `{\"ncols\": 1, \"rows\": [...], \"cycles\": C}` as one line of JSON; on\n`examples/data.json` that is 26 rows and 136 cycles.
