[MiniVM docs](README.md) › Language\n\n# Language\n\nThis page gives the syntax of MiniVM programs: lines, comments, opcodes,\nregisters, operands and literals.\n\n## Programs\n\nA program is straight-line: its instructions run once each, in order. Each\nline holds one instruction. A `;` starts a comment, which runs to the end of\nthe line; a line may hold only a comment, or be blank. Spaces and tabs are\ninterchangeable: they separate the opcode from its operands, and may indent a\nline or surround an operand.\n\n```text\n; Ids and amounts of orders over 100.\nload   id, orders.o_id\nload   amt, orders.o_amt\ngt     m, amt, 100      ; NULL where o_amt is NULL\nidx    i, m\ngather a, id, i\ngather b, amt, i\nout    a, b\n```\n\nThe program must end with its only `OUT`; see [Program rules](running.md#program\n-rules).                                                                        \n## Instructions\n\nAn instruction is an opcode followed by comma-separated operands:\n\n```text\nOP dest, operand, ...\n```\n\nOpcodes are case-insensitive: `gt`, `Gt` and `GT` are the same instruction.\nSo are the keywords `NULL`, `TRUE`, `FALSE`, `ASC`, `DESC`, `NF`, `NL` and\n`NULLEQ`.\nEach opcode's operands are given on its page in the\n[instruction reference](instructions/README.md).\n\n## Registers\n\nRegister names are identifiers, such as `r1`, `amt` or `_t0`: a letter or `_`,\nfollowed by letters, digits and `_`. Register names are case-sensitive, and a\nkeyword can't be a register name. A register holds a column or a group set\n([Values](values.md#columns-and-group-sets)) and can be overwritten.\n\n## Operands\n\nAn operand is one of:\n\n| Operand | Example | Used by |\n|---|---|---|\n| register | `amt` | every instruction |\n| literal | `100.00` | element-wise instructions, `FILL`, integer operands such \nas `LEFT`'s `n` |                                                               | `table.column` | `orders.o_amt` | [`LOAD`](instructions/columns.md#load) |\n| sort key | `amt DESC NL` | [`SORT`, `TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys)\n |                                                                              | `NULLEQ` | `NULLEQ` | [`NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) \n|                                                                               \n## Literals\n\n| Literal | Type | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| `42`, `-7` | INT | must fit in 128 bits |\n| `12.50` | NUM | must be exact, in the [NUM range](values.md#num-range) |\n| `'it''s'` | STR | a quote inside the string is written twice |\n| `#2024-01-31#` | DATE | years 0001 to 9999 |\n| `NULL` | NULL | |\n| `TRUE`, `FALSE` | BOOL | |\n\nA literal stands for that value at every row.\n\n## Integer operands\n\nSome operands must be integer literals rather than registers: `n` and `len`\n(`LEFT`, `SUBSTR`, `SLICE`, `TOPK`) are non-negative, and `SUBSTR`'s `start` is\nat least 1. They may be arbitrarily large; a count larger than the input means\nall of it.\n[MiniVM docs](README.md) › Values\n\n# Values\n\nThis page describes MiniVM's values and types, what a register holds, and how\nvalues are ordered and compared.\n\n## Types\n\n| Type | Values | Literal |\n|---|---|---|\n| INT | exact 128-bit integer; a result outside -2^127 .. 2^127-1 is an error | \n`42` |                                                                          | NUM | decimal: see [NUM range](#num-range) | `12.50` |\n| STR | string | `'it''s'` |\n| DATE | calendar date | `#2024-01-31#` |\n| BOOL | `FALSE` or `TRUE` | `TRUE` |\n\n`NULL` is a value of its own, written `NULL`. Unless an instruction says\notherwise, an element-wise result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`\n([element-wise instructions](instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions)).\n\nLiteral syntax is in [Literals](language.md#literals). Stored columns have\ntype INT, NUM, STR or DATE ([table sets](running.md#table-sets)).\n\n## NUM range\n\nA NUM is below 1e28 in magnitude and has at most 28 digits after the point,\nand its digits without the point, read as an integer, are at most\n2^96 - 1 = 79228162514264337593543950335: 28 or 29 significant digits.\nA NUM keeps its digits after the point, so `1.0` and `1.00` are equal but\nprint differently.\n\nA NUM literal or stored value must be such a number exactly; trailing zeros\nafter the point are dropped as far as needed. A NUM result is rounded half to\neven to the most digits after the point that fit, and a result of magnitude\n1e28 or more is the error `numeric overflow`. Where an INT meets a NUM in\narithmetic, and in `DIV`, an INT operand above 2^96 - 1 in magnitude is that\nerror too, even if the result would fit.\n\n## Columns and group sets\n\nA register holds either:\n\n- a **column**: a vector of values; or\n- a **group set**: a grouping of rows, made by\n  [`GROUP`](instructions/grouping.md#group) or [`GALL`](instructions/grouping.md\n#gall)                                                                            and read by the other [grouping instructions](instructions/grouping.md).\n\nRegisters can be overwritten.\n\n## Ordering\n\nThese instructions compare values:\n\n- [`EQ`, `NE`, `LT`, `LE`, `GT`, `GE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) \nand [`IS`](instructions/logic.md#is)                                            - [`SORT`](instructions/sorting.md#sort) and [`TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#to\npk)                                                                             - the joins [`NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin)\n- [`GMIN`, `GMAX`](instructions/grouping.md#gmin-gmax)\n\nThey order values as follows:\n\n| Values | Order |\n|---|---|\n| INT and NUM | by numeric value, exactly at any magnitude; INT and NUM mix |\n| STR | by bytes |\n| DATE | by date |\n| BOOL | `FALSE < TRUE` |\n\nComparing any other mix of types, such as STR with INT or DATE with NUM, is an\nerror.\n\nString comparison is exact: there is no case folding, and trailing spaces\ncount, so `'ab'` and `'ab '` differ, as do `'ab'` and `'AB'`.\n\nHow each instruction treats `NULL` is given on its page; for sorts, see\n[sort keys](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys).\n[MiniVM docs](README.md) › Running\n\n# Running\n\nThis page gives the rules every program must follow, what happens on an error,\nhow to run a program with `bin/minivm`, and the JSON format of the tables it\nreads.\n\n## Program rules\n\nThe last instruction must be the program's only [`OUT`](instructions/columns.md#\nout).                                                                           \n| Limit | Value |\n|---|---|\n| instructions per program | at most 20,000 |\n| values held by one register | at most 4,000,000 (a join's output counts) |\n| values held by all registers together | at most 64,000,000; a long string coun\nts as several values (about 1 per 32 bytes) |                                   | work per run | roughly 300,000,000 [cycles](cycles.md); see below |\n| rows per table | at most 10,000 |\n| program file | at most 4 MiB |\n| table-set file | at most 32 MiB and 2,000,000 JSON values |\n\nThe work limit stops runaway programs. It counts a run's cycles, but `HJOIN`\nand `GROUP` and copying long strings use it up faster than their cycles\nsuggest, so such programs stop somewhat sooner. Exceeding it, like any other\nlimit, is an error. It has no effect on the cycles reported for a run that\nfinishes.\n\n## Errors\n\nAny error stops the program. No result is printed; the error goes to stderr\nand `bin/minivm` exits with status 1.\n\n## Command line\n\n```sh\nbin/minivm PROGRAM.mini TABLES.json\nbin/minivm --schema TABLES.json\n```\n\nruns the program in `PROGRAM.mini` on the [table set](#table-sets) in\n`TABLES.json`. On success it prints one line of JSON to stdout and exits 0:\n\n```json\n{\"ncols\": N, \"rows\": [...], \"cycles\": C}\n```\n\n- `ncols` is the number of `OUT` operands.\n- `rows` is the result, one array of `ncols` values per row.\n  `NULL` is `null` and a BOOL is `true` or `false`. An INT is a JSON integer,\n  or a string of its digits outside -2^63 .. 2^63-1. A NUM is a string that keep\ns                                                                                 its digits after the point (`\"250.00\"`), a STR a string, and a DATE a string\n  `\"YYYY-MM-DD\"`.\n- `cycles` is the program's cost ([Cycles](cycles.md)).\n\n| Exit status | Meaning |\n|---|---|\n| 0 | success; the result is on stdout |\n| 1 | error; the message is on stderr |\n| 2 | wrong number of arguments; a usage line is on stderr |\n\nWith the program from [Language](language.md#programs) saved as\n`over100.mini` and the [example table set](#example) as `orders.json`:\n\n```sh\n$ bin/minivm over100.mini orders.json\n{\"ncols\":2,\"rows\":[[1,\"250.00\"]],\"cycles\":42}\n```\n\n`bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json` prints the table set's [schema file](#schema-f\niles)                                                                           as one line of JSON instead of running a program.\n\nA program that compares a DATE with an INT stops with an error:\n\n```text\nLOAD d, orders.o_date\nGT   m, d, 5\nOUT  m\n```\n\n```sh\n$ bin/minivm bad.mini orders.json\nerror: line 2: GT: expected a number, got DATE\n```\n\n## Table sets\n\nA table set is a JSON object mapping each table name to its columns and rows:\n\n```json\n{\"<table>\": {\"columns\": [{\"name\": \"c\", \"type\": \"INT|NUM|STR|DATE\"}], \"rows\": [[.\n..], ...]}}                                                                     ```\n\n- Table and column names are identifiers (letters, digits and `_`, not starting\n  with a digit), compared without regard to case. Duplicate names are an error.\n- `columns` lists each column's `name` and `type`, one of `INT`, `NUM`, `STR`, `\nDATE`.                                                                          - `rows` lists each row as an array of values, one per column, in column order.\n  A table without `rows` is empty.\n- A table may also declare [constraints](#constraints).\n- Any key other than those shown or listed there is an error, as is a repeated k\ney.                                                                             - A table holds at most 10,000 rows.\n- INT values are JSON integers that fit in 32 bits.\n- NUM values may be JSON numbers or strings. They must be exact, in the\n  [NUM range](values.md#num-range).\n- Dates are strings `\"YYYY-MM-DD\"`, years 0001 to 9999.\n- JSON `null` is `NULL`.\n\nA program reads a stored column with `LOAD d, table.column` ([`LOAD`](instructio\nns/columns.md#load)).                                                           \n### Constraints\n\nA table may declare what its rows guarantee. `bin/minivm` checks every declared\nconstraint when it reads the table set, and a table set that breaks one is an er\nror.                                                                            \n| Key | Example | Guarantee |\n|---|---|---|\n| `key` | `[\"l_order\", \"l_no\"]` | the columns are never `NULL`, and no two rows \nagree on all of them |                                                          | `not_null` | `[\"p_price\"]` | the columns are never `NULL` |\n| `refs` | `{\"l_prod\": \"products.p_id\"}` | every non-NULL value of the column is\n a value of the other column, which must be its table's whole `key` and have the same type (INT and NUM may refer to each other) |                              | `check` | `{\"l_qty\": [1, 500]}` | every non-NULL value lies between the bounds\n, inclusive; `null` leaves a side open; INT, NUM and DATE columns only |        | `sorted` | `[\"l_order\", \"l_no\"]` | the rows are stored in ascending order of t\nhe columns, as `ASC NF` sorts them |                                            \nValues are compared as in [Ordering](values.md#ordering), so NUM keys `1.0` and\n`1.00` are the same key. Column names in constraints are compared without regard\nto case, and naming a column twice in one constraint is an error. A table may re\nfer to itself.                                                                  \n```json\n{\n  \"orders\": {\"columns\": [{\"name\": \"o_id\", \"type\": \"INT\"}], \"key\": [\"o_id\"], \"row\ns\": [[1], [2]]},                                                                  \"lines\": {\n    \"columns\": [{\"name\": \"l_order\", \"type\": \"INT\"}, {\"name\": \"l_qty\", \"type\": \"I\nNT\"}],                                                                              \"refs\": {\"l_order\": \"orders.o_id\"}, \"check\": {\"l_qty\": [1, null]}, \"sorted\":\n [\"l_order\"],                                                                       \"rows\": [[1, 3], [1, 1], [2, 5]]\n  }\n}\n```\n\n### Example\n\n```json\n{\n  \"orders\": {\n    \"columns\": [\n      {\"name\": \"o_id\",     \"type\": \"INT\"},\n      {\"name\": \"o_amt\",    \"type\": \"NUM\"},\n      {\"name\": \"o_date\",   \"type\": \"DATE\"},\n      {\"name\": \"o_status\", \"type\": \"STR\"}\n    ],\n    \"rows\": [\n      [1, 250.00,   \"2024-01-31\", \"shipped\"],\n      [2, \"99.5\",   \"2024-02-01\", \"\"],\n      [3, null,     \"2024-02-03\", null]\n    ]\n  }\n}\n```\n\n## Schema files\n\n`bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json` describes a table set without its rows: each t\nable's                                                                          columns and [constraints](#constraints), as in the table set, plus a `stats` obj\nect                                                                             summarizing its rows:\n\n```json\n{\"<table>\": {\"columns\": [...], \"key\": [...], ..., \"stats\": {\"rows\": N, \"columns\"\n: {\"<column>\": {\"nulls\": N, \"distinct\": N, \"min\": v, \"max\": v, \"common\": [[v, N], ...], ...}}}}}                                                                ```\n\nThe constraints hold for every table set with this schema; the stats describe on\nly this one.                                                                    \n| Stats field | Meaning |\n|---|---|\n| `rows` | rows in the table |\n| `nulls` | `NULL` values in the column |\n| `distinct` | distinct non-NULL values, compared as in [Ordering](values.md#ord\nering) |                                                                        | `min`, `max` | least and greatest non-NULL value; `null` if there is none |\n| `avg_bytes` | STR only: mean bytes of the non-NULL values, rounded to 2 decima\nl places; 0 if there are none |                                                 | `common` | up to 8 values that occur more than once, most frequent first (ties\n in value order), with their counts |                                           | `histogram` | INT, NUM and DATE only, if any value is non-NULL: 11 bounds of 1\n0 equal-count buckets of the sorted non-NULL values, from `min` to `max` |      [MiniVM docs](README.md) › Cycles\n\n# Cycles\n\nThis page defines how many cycles a program costs. A program's cost is the sum\nof its instructions' costs, and `bin/minivm` reports it as `cycles`\n([Running](running.md#command-line)).\n\n## Base cost\n\nEvery instruction costs 4, plus the cost given for it in the\n[cost table](#cost-table). `OUT` costs only the 4.\n\nA run is stopped with an error if it does too much work; see the\n[work limit](running.md#program-rules).\n\n## String bytes\n\nThe string bytes of a value are the number of bytes in it if it is a STR, and\n0 otherwise (including `NULL`).\n\nAn [element-wise instruction](instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions)\ncosts, for each element of its result, a base amount plus string bytes:\n\n| Instructions | Base per element |\n|---|---|\n| `DIV` `IDIV` `MOD` | 6 |\n| `TRUNC` `YEAR` `MONTH` `DAY` `DOW` `DATEADD` `DATEDIFF` | 2 |\n| every other element-wise instruction | 1 |\n\n| Instructions | String bytes per element |\n|---|---|\n| comparisons: `EQ` `NE` `LT` `LE` `GT` `GE` `IS` | the bytes of the shorter ope\nrand |                                                                          | `LEN` | the bytes of its operand |\n| `ISNULL` `NVL` `IF` `NULLIF` `NULLIFE` | nothing |\n| every other element-wise instruction | 1 per byte of each string operand (lite\nrals included) and of its result |                                              \nA literal operand counts at every element, like the value it stands for.\n\n## Comparisons\n\n`SORT` and `TOPK` compare rows on their sort keys\n([sort keys](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys)). One comparison of two rows\ncosts, for each key examined until one differs, 2 plus the bytes of the\nshorter string.\n\nFor example, on a table `t` whose STR column `s` and INT column `n` hold the\nrows `('ab', 5)` and `('ab', 7)`, comparing the two rows on keys\n`s ASC NL, n ASC NL` costs 2 + 2 for the first key, which is equal, and 2 + 0\nfor the second, which differs: 6 in all. Sorting the two rows takes that one\ncomparison:\n\n```text\nLOAD s, t.s\nLOAD n, t.n\nSORT o, s ASC NL, n ASC NL\nOUT  o\n```\n\ncosts (4 + 2) + (4 + 2) + (4 + 2 x 2 rows + 6) + 4 = 30 cycles.\n\n## [`MUL`](instructions/arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) [`NEG`](instructions/arithmetic.md#neg) [`WRAP`](instructions/arithmetic.md#wrap) | 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals [`MOD`](instructions/arithmetic.md#mod) | 6 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |                     | [`TRUNC`](instructions/arithmetic.md#trunc) | 2 per element, plus 1 per byte o\nf each string operand (literals included) and of its result |                   | Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                           \n| Instruction | Result |\n|---|---|\n| [`GROUP g, k, ...`](#group) | group set: rows with equal keys share a group |\n| [`GALL g, s`](#gall) | group set: one group holding every row of `s` |\n| [`GID d, g`](#gid) | group number of each row |\n| [`GFIRST d, g`](#gfirst) | position of each group's first row |\n| [`GCOUNT d, g`](#gcount) | rows per group |\n| [`GCOUNTV d, g, s`](#gcountv) | non-NULL values of `s` per group |\n| [`GSUM d, g, s`](#gsum) | sum of non-NULL values per group |\n| [`GMIN d, g, s` / `GMAX`](#gmin-gmax) | least / greatest non-NULL value per gr\noup |                                                                           \n## Group sets\n\nA register holds either a column or a group set ([values](../values.md#columns-a\nnd-group-sets)). A group set assigns each of its rows a group number; groups are numbered from 0 in order of first appearance. [`GROUP`](#group) and [`GALL`](#gall) produce a group set. [`GID`](#gid) returns a column with one value per row; the aggregates [`GFIRST`](#gfirst) through [`GMAX`](#gmin-gmax) return a column with one value per group, the value for group `k` at position `k`. The `s` operand of an aggregate is a column over the same rows as the group set; a different length is an error.                                                            \nAggregate columns of the same group set line up with each other. To label each g\nroup with its key, gather the key at [`GFIRST`](#gfirst). Orders per status:    \n```text\nLOAD   st, orders.o_status\nGROUP  g, st\nGFIRST f, g\nGATHER key, st, f\nGCOUNT n, g\nOUT    key, n\n```\n\nOn `examples/data.json` this prints `[[\"open\",7],[\"closed\",12],[\"shipped\",11]]`.\n\n## `GROUP`\n\n```text\nGROUP g, k, ...\n```\n\nSets `g` to a group set over the rows of the key columns `k, ...`: rows with equ\nal keys share a group, and NULL equals NULL. All key columns must have the same length. Keys are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering): INT and NUM mix (`1` and `1.00` share a group), and a key column holding values that can't be compared (e.g. STR and INT) is an error.                                       \n**Cycles:** per row: 6 plus the string bytes of its keys ([rules](../cycles.md#s\ntring-bytes)).                                                                  \n## `GALL`\n\n```text\nGALL g, s\n```\n\nSets `g` to a group set with one group holding every row of `s`, even when `s` i\ns empty.                                                                        \n**Cycles:** 1 per row.\n\n## `GID`\n\n```text\nGID d, g\n```\n\nSets `d` to the group number of each row of `g`.\n\n**Cycles:** 1 per row.\n\n## `GFIRST`\n\n```text\nGFIRST d, g\n```\n\nSets `d` to the position of each group's first row. The result is NULL for the g\nroup of an empty `GALL`.                                                        \n**Cycles:** 1 per row.\n\n## `GCOUNT`\n\n```text\nGCOUNT d, g\n```\n\nSets `d` to the number of rows in each group.\n\n**Cycles:** 2 per row.\n\n## `GCOUNTV`\n\n```text\nGCOUNTV d, g, s\n```\n\nSets `d` to the number of non-NULL values of `s` in each group.\n\n**Cycles:** 2 per row.\n\n## `GSUM`\n\n```text\nGSUM d, g, s\n```\n\nSets `d` to the sum of the non-NULL values of `s` in each group: INT when all ar\ne INT, else NUM. The result is NULL for a group with no non-NULL values. A NUM sum is computed exactly, with as many digits after the point as the value with the most, and rounded once as in [NUM range](../values.md#num-range), so it doesn't depend on the order of the rows. Only each group's total is checked: a total outside the INT or NUM range is the error `numeric overflow`, whatever the running sums along the way.                                                           \n**Cycles:** 2 per row.\n\n## `GMIN`, `GMAX`\n\n```text\nGMIN d, g, s\nGMAX d, g, s\n```\n\nSets `d` to the least (`GMIN`) or greatest (`GMAX`) non-NULL value of `s` in eac\nh group, the first of equals: of `1`, `1.0` and `1.00`, whichever comes first. Values are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering). The result is NULL for a group with no non-NULL values.                                             \n**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus the bytes of each non-NULL string ([rules](../cycles\n.md#string-bytes)).                                                             [MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Joins\n\n# Join instructions\n\n`NLJOIN` and `HJOIN` pair up the rows of two key columns whose keys are equal an\nd return the pairs as two position columns. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                                                  \n| Instruction | Result |\n|---|---|\n| [`NLJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]`](#nljoin-hjoin) | positions of all pairs w\nith `lk[i] = rk[j]` |                                                           | [`HJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]`](#nljoin-hjoin) | same result as `NLJOIN` |\n\n## `NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`\n\n```text\nNLJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]\nHJOIN  li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]\n```\n\nFinds all pairs `(i, j)` with `lk[i] = rk[j]`, ordered by `i` then `j`. Sets `li\n` to the positions into `lk` and `ri` to the positions into `rk`, one entry per pair; if `li` and `ri` are the same register, it holds the positions into `rk`. Keys are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering): a non-NULL left key that can't be compared with a non-NULL right key (e.g. STR with INT) is an error. A NULL key matches no key, unless the optional `NULLEQ` flag is given, in which case NULL keys match each other. `HJOIN` gives the same result as `NLJOIN`, errors included; only the cost differs.                                            \n**Cycles (`NLJOIN`):** per pair of rows: 1 plus the bytes of the shorter string \nkey ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)); plus 2 per output pair.               \n**Cycles (`HJOIN`):** per row of either side: 6 plus its key's string bytes ([ru\nles](../cycles.md#string-bytes)); plus 2 per output pair.                       \n### Example\n\n[`GATHER`](columns.md#gather) through `li` picks columns of the left rows and th\nrough `ri` columns of the right rows, giving one row per pair. Customers with their region's name:                                                              \n```text\nLOAD   reg, customers.c_region\nLOAD   code, regions.r_code\nHJOIN  li, ri, reg, code\nLOAD   cname, customers.c_name\nLOAD   rname, regions.r_name\nGATHER c, cname, li\nGATHER r, rname, ri\nOUT    c, r\n```\n\nOn `examples/data.json` this prints `[[\"Cy\",\"Southern\"],[\"Dee\",\"West Coast\"],[\"E\nve\",\"Southern\"], ...]`.                                                         [MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Sorting\n\n# Sorting instructions\n\n`SORT` and `TOPK` order the rows of one or more key columns and return positions\n, which [`GATHER`](columns.md#gather) applies to any column of the same rows. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                \n| Instruction | Result |\n|---|---|\n| [`SORT d, key, ...`](#sort) | positions of the rows in stable sorted order |\n| [`TOPK d, n, key, ...`](#topk) | the first `n` positions of the same order |\n\n## `SORT`\n\n```text\nSORT d, key, ...\n```\n\nSets `d` to the positions of the rows in stable sorted order by the [sort keys](\n#sort-keys).                                                                    \n**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus every comparison of a stable top-down merge sort ([c\nomparison cost](../cycles.md#comparisons)).                                     \n## `TOPK`\n\n```text\nTOPK d, n, key, ...\n```\n\nSets `d` to the first `n` positions of the order `SORT` would produce for the sa\nme keys (all of them if there are fewer rows). `n` is an integer literal.       \n**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus every comparison of a bounded insertion buffer (each\n row is compared with the current `n`-th, then placed by binary search) ([comparison cost](../cycles.md#comparisons)), plus 1 per buffered row shifted.         \n## Sort keys\n\n```text\nreg ASC|DESC NF|NL\n```\n\nA sort key is a register followed by a direction and a NULL placement, separated\n by spaces or tabs; all three parts are required. All key columns must have the same length. Rows are ordered by the first key, then by each following key among rows the earlier keys leave equal.                                             \n- `ASC` orders values from least to greatest, `DESC` reverses the order of value\ns. Values are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering).                 - `NF` puts NULLs first and `NL` puts them last, whatever the direction.\n- Ties keep their input order.\n\nCustomers by credit, highest first with NULLs last, then by name:\n\n```text\nLOAD   name, customers.c_name\nLOAD   credit, customers.c_credit\nSORT   p, credit DESC NL, name ASC NF\nGATHER n, name, p\nGATHER c, credit, p\nOUT    n, c\n```\n[MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Strings\n\n# Strings\n\nElement-wise operations on STR values. All instructions on this page follow the \n[element-wise rules](README.md#element-wise-instructions): the result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`. Lengths and positions count characters; string-byte costs count bytes ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)).                         \n| Instruction | Result |\n|---|---|\n| [`UPPER d, s`](#upper) | upper case (Unicode) |\n| [`RTRIM d, s`](#rtrim-trim) / [`TRIM d, s`](#rtrim-trim) | without trailing / \nleading and trailing spaces |                                                   | [`LEFT d, s, n`](#left) | first `n` characters |\n| [`SUBSTR d, s, start, len`](#substr) | `len` characters from 1-based `start` |\n| [`LEN d, s`](#len) | number of characters |\n| [`CAT d, a, b`](#cat) | concatenation |\n\n## `UPPER`\n\n```text\nUPPER d, s\n```\n\n`s` in upper case, by Unicode's full case mapping, which can change the number o\nf characters: `UPPER('straße')` is `'STRASSE'`.                                 \n**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` and of the result ([rules](../\ncycles.md#string-bytes)).                                                       \n## `RTRIM`, `TRIM`\n\n```text\nRTRIM d, s\nTRIM  d, s\n```\n\n`s` without trailing spaces (`RTRIM`), or without leading and trailing spaces (`\nTRIM`). Only `' '` counts as a space.                                           \n**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` and of the result ([rules](../\ncycles.md#string-bytes)).                                                       \n## `LEFT`\n\n```text\nLEFT d, s, n\n```\n\nThe first `n` characters of `s` (all of `s` if it is shorter). `n` is a non-nega\ntive [integer literal](../language.md#integer-operands).                        \n**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` and of the result ([rules](../\ncycles.md#string-bytes)).                                                       \n## `SUBSTR`\n\n```text\nSUBSTR d, s, start, len\n```\n\n`len` characters of `s`, starting at the 1-based position `start` (fewer if `s` \nends first). `start` (at least 1) and `len` are [integer literals](../language.md#integer-operands).                                                            \n**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` and of the result ([rules](../\ncycles.md#string-bytes)).                                                       \n## `LEN`\n\n```text\nLEN d, s\n```\n\nINT: the number of characters in `s`.\n\n**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` ([rules](../cycles.md#string-b\nytes)).                                                                         \n## `CAT`\n\n```text\nCAT d, a, b\n```\n\nThe concatenation of `a` and `b`.\n\n**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `a`, of `b` (literals included) an\nd of the result ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)).                           \n## Example\n\nGiven a table `t` whose STR column `s` holds `' ab '`, `''` and `'Zoë'`:\n\n```text\nLOAD  s, t.s\nTRIM  u, s\nCAT   c, u, '!'\nLEN   l, c\nOUT   c, l\n```\n\nprints `{\"ncols\":2,\"rows\":[[\"ab!\",3],[\"!\",1],[\"Zoë!\",4]],\"cycles\":73}`. `'Zoë!'`\n has 4 characters but 5 bytes: `CAT` costs 1 + 4 + 1 + 5 = 11 cycles on that row, and `LEN` costs 1 + 5. For us: original vs optimized on the same VM. Csmith's lesson: generated programs must avoid UB (for us, programs that error) and print enough output for differences to show up. Our version is a test-based check per program.\n- **STOKE** (superoptimizer): cheap tests filter candidates, then a formal check runs, and each counterexample becomes a new test (CEGIS loop). SQLancer: **TLP** (a query's result = union of its results under `p`, `NOT p`, `p IS NULL`), **NoREC** (compare against a form the optimizer can't optimize), **PQS** (pick a row and check it appears in the result). For us: the original program *is* the non-optimizing reference. TLP-style 3-way NULL partitions are a good model for adversarial data.\n- **Test-case reduction**: C-Reduce / delta debugging, guided by an \"interestingness\" predicate. Shrink the dataset rows (children before parents, to keep `refs` valid) and then the program lines, while the diff still reproduces.\n- **Mutation testing of the oracle**: plant known faults in the optimizer and measure the kill rate. Also confirm that correct rewrites are *not* killed, so false positives are measured too.\n\n**Verified VM facts that matter for the evaluator**\n- The `bin/minivm` wrapper runs `xattr` on every call: **43 ms serial, about 86 runs/s on 16 workers**. Calling `bin/minivm-macos-aarch64` directly takes **8.8 ms, about 420 runs/s**. The parallel speedup is only about 5x, likely due to process-spawn overhead.\n- Output is deterministic: md5 matched over 3 runs. A 10k×10k `NLJOIN` producing a 2M-row output takes 425 ms and prints 13 MB of JSON (`HJOIN`: 188 ms).\n- `--schema` rejects data that breaks a constraint (duplicate key, out-of-order `sorted`, INT outside 32 bits) with exit 1. Use it as the data-generator gate. `sorted` is checked as `ASC NF`, so NULLs come first.\n- NUM keeps its scale: `GMIN` over `1.0`/`1.00` returns whichever comes first. `GSUM` scale = the largest scale among its inputs (`\"2.00\"`). `ADD x, 0.000` keeps `\"1.0\"`. `DIV 3,1` prints `\"3\"`, a NUM string with no point, so the type is not visible in the output.\n- An error gives exit 1 and nothing on stdout. Errors depend on the data: `DIV` by zero only on rows that are actually used.\n- Empty table: `GALL`+`GCOUNT` gives 1 row `[0,null,null]`. `GROUP` gives 0 rows. `UPPER('straße')`→`STRASSE`, so `LEFT∘UPPER ≠ UPPER∘LEFT`. `DATEADD 9999-12-31,1` is an error.\n- The schema's `stats` describe one dataset only. The optimizer must be correct for **any** data that meets the constraints.\n\n## Risks\n\n- **False alarm on order.** A program \"specifies order\" only if its OUT rows come, through GATHER, IDX or SLICE, from a `SORT`/`TOPK`. Rows tied on the sort keys keep their *input* order, and a correct join reorder can legally change that order. Comparing tied rows strictly would flag correct optimizers.\n- **Ties at a cut-off** (`SORT`+`SLICE`, `TOPK`, or `GFIRST` after a non-total sort for de-dup): a correct optimizer can return a different tied row. This is ambiguous in the spec. Choose lenient handling and document it.\n- **Type is not visible in output.** STR `\"2.00\"` and NUM `\"2.00\"` print the same. Numeric tolerance on strings that look like numbers can hide a real STR change. INT `3` vs NUM `\"3\"` must count as equal.\n- **Relative-only tolerance near zero.** `0` vs `1e-28`, e.g. a DIV-rounding residue, fails a strict `|a-b| ≤ 1e-6·max`. This is a spec-conformant flag, but it may look harsh.\n- **Optimizer timing under load.** Running 16 VMs in parallel inflates the optimizer's wall time, which can produce a false \">1 s\" failure.\n- **Missed bugs (the evaluator wrongly passes a bad optimizer):**\n  - The data generator only produces data that looks like the stats.\n  - No NULLs in nullable `refs`/`check` columns.\n  - No duplicates in non-key join columns.\n  - No empty or 1-row tables.\n  - Programs whose output is always empty.\n- **Budget:** a slow optimizer (up to 1 s × N programs) dominates the run time, not the VM. Large join outputs make JSON parsing in Python the bottleneck.\n\n## Recommendations\n\n**Proving it WRONG within 2 min**\n- Resolve the native binary the same way the wrapper does, with a fallback to `bin/minivm`. That gives about 420 runs/s, so 90 s ≈ 35k VM runs. Timeouts: 5 s per VM run, 2 s per optimizer call (flag at more than 1 s).\n- **Corpus:** the 8 examples, their mutants, and type-inferred generated programs. Keep a program only if the original succeeds on at least 1 dataset and gives non-empty output on at least 1. Order the work as: killer datasets first, then examples, then generated programs (STOKE-style).\n- **Data:** run `--schema` on every generated dataset and require its columns and constraints to equal the target schema, ignoring stats. Give the optimizer the schema of dataset D0, then test it on D1..Dk, whose stats deliberately differ (nulls where D0 had none, values beyond D0's min/max, duplicates where D0 was distinct).\n- **Adversarial values:**\n  - NULL in every nullable column, including nullable FKs and `check` columns.\n  - Ties in sort keys; duplicate join keys.\n  - `''` vs NULL; `'Open '`/`'OPEN'`/`'open'`; `ß`/multibyte strings.\n  - `1.0`/`1.00`; zeros in divisor-like columns.\n  - Values exactly on the `check` bounds; dates `0001-01-01`, `9999-12-31`, Feb 29.\n  - Empty, 1-row and max-fan-out tables.\n- Call the optimizer once per program, all calls in parallel, and cache the output. Fan out VM runs on 16 workers. **Exit early** on the first confirmed defect: re-run once to rule out flakiness, save the repro to `eval_out/`, exit 1. A watchdog at about 100 s stops new work and exits with the verdict so far.\n- If time remains, shrink the repro with delta debugging (≤10 s cap).\n\n**Not flagging a CORRECT optimizer**\n- Skip a (program, dataset) pair when the original errors or hits a VM limit. It is a defect when the original succeeds and the optimized program errors, fails to parse, times out, or `ncols` differs.\n- **Order:** do a static dataflow check for whether order is specified.\n  - If order is unspecified, compare as multisets: sort both sides by a canonical key.\n  - If order is specified, compare row by row, but canonical-sort *inside* runs of rows tied on the sort keys. If the keys are not in OUT, recover them by running an instrumented original with the sort keys appended to OUT.\n  - Treat a diff at a TOPK/SLICE tie boundary as ambiguous: warn, don't fail.\n- **Values:**\n  - Exact match first.\n  - Both values numeric (JSON int, or a string matching `^-?\\d+(\\.\\d+)?$`): compare as `Decimal` with `|a−b| ≤ 1e-6·max(|a|,|b|)`, so `2.0`=`2.00` and `3`=`\"3\"`.\n  - NULL only equals NULL. STR, DATE and BOOL must match exactly.\n  - Better: infer OUT column types statically so numeric tolerance is never applied to STR.\n- **Determinism:** fixed seed, sorted work lists, no wall-clock dependence in the verdict, only the deadline. Time the optimizer outside the VM fan-out, or re-time it alone before flagging \">1 s\".\n- **Meta-eval:** `cat` (identity) and known-correct rewrites must give 0 alarms. Correct rewrites to test:\n  - reorder unsorted output\n  - change NUM scale\n  - TOPK ↔ SORT+SLICE\n  - INT→NUM with the same value\n  - swap the HJOIN/NLJOIN sides with a re-sort\n\n  Bad mutants must give 100% kill:\n  - drop a filter\n  - ASC↔DESC, NF↔NL\n  - drop NULLEQ; IS→EQ\n  - `NOT GT` → `LE` (wrong under NULL)\n  - move DIV before the filter\n  - swap LEFT and UPPER\n  - remove an inner join on a nullable FK\n  - GALL→GROUP (wrong on an empty table)\n  - TOPK n±1\n  - assume stats are constraints (drop an ISNULL check because nulls=0)\n", "file_path": "/Users/skodi/Desktop/take-home-assessment/notes/research_evaluator.md"}, "client_side_execute": true, "classification": {"file_facts": {"in_scope": false, "operation": "FILE_OP_WRITE", "paths": ["/Users/skodi/Desktop/take-home-assessment/notes/research_evaluator.md"]}, "reasons": ["File write"], "risk_level": "RISK_LEVEL_MEDIUM"}}}], "model": "claude-opus-5-5", "thinkingEffort": "medium", "createdOn": 1794344386319, "summaryRevision": "", "autoRouterSelected": false}

NULL vs non-NULL is a defect. |\n    55|| Q4 | Is a different `ncols` or column order a defect? | Yes, always. |\n    56|| Q5 | Optimized program errors, times out (>1 s) or hits a VM limit where the original succeeds? | Defect. |\n    57|| Q6 | Optimizer crashes or prints garbage? | Defect (counted as \"optimizer failure\"). |\n    58|| Q7 | Can we rely on `stats`? | Only for **cost choices** (HJOIN vs NLJOIN, which side to filter), never for correctness. Stats describe one dataset. |\n    59|| Q8 | \"Faster\" measured how? | `cycles` reported by `bin/minivm`, on the example data and on generated data. |\n    60|| Q9 | Can the optimizer run `bin/minivm`? | Not required, and we don't depend on it (the grader may not provide it to `optimize`). |\n    61|| Q10 | Hidden programs: same shape as the examples? | Assume \"legacy\" SQL-ish plans: wide GATHER fan-outs, late filters, self-joins, redundant sorts, dead columns. |\n    62|\n    63|---\n    64|\n    65|## 3. Optimizer design\n    66|\n    67|**Pipeline:** parse → SSA IR (rename registers, def-use, value metadata: source table, row domain, type, nullability, sortedness) → passes to a fixpoint → cost check → emit.\n    68|**Global guard:** if the optimized program's estimated cost ≥ the original's, or any pass throws, emit the original.\n    69|\n    70|### Rewrites ranked by (gain ÷ risk)\n    71|\n    72|| Rank | Rewrite | Gain [est] | Risk | Safety rule |\n    73||---|---|---|---|---|\n    74|| 1 | **Dead-code elimination** (unused LOAD/GATHER/string ops; e.g. q7 `upper r14`, `dow r15`) | 5–25% | very low | Removing instructions only removes possible errors. Never remove `OUT`. |\n    75|| 2 | **GATHER composition and sinking**: `GATHER(GATHER(s,i),j)` → `GATHER(s, GATHER(i,j))`; carry *index vectors* through joins and filters and gather payload columns only at the end, only for columns that reach `OUT` | 20–50% on wide plans (q1, q4, q5) | low | Identity of index composition. Indices are in range by construction (same as the original). |\n    76|| 3 | **CSE**: duplicate LOADs and identical ops (q2 loads `l_disc` twice) | small | very low | Pure ops are deterministic. |\n    77|| 4 | **Late materialization of element-wise ops**: compute `f(x)` after filters (`f(GATHER(x,i)) = GATHER(f(x),i)`), only on surviving rows | 20–40% (q1, q4, q7 string ops) | low | Evaluating on a *subset* of rows can only remove errors. **Never** move an op onto rows it wasn't evaluated on, and never onto a join-expanded domain larger than the original (cost check). |\n    78|| 5 | **Constraint rewrites**: `SORT` keys = prefix of `sorted` ASC NF on an unpermuted table → identity; predicate always TRUE by `not_null` + `check` (q1 `GE l_qty,1`) → drop it; `key` uniqueness ⇒ joins are at most 1:1, so a GROUP on key cols is identity | 5–15% | low-med | Uses only declared constraints. Must also prove the column isn't permuted or filtered in between (sortedness survives IDX/GATHER-by-ascending-index only). |\n    79|| 6 | **Filter pushdown below joins** (q4 filters after 4 joins) | 30–70% on q4-like plans | med | Filtering the left side with IDX preserves the (i, j) output order. Applies only when the predicate depends on one side. Cast-free: same ops, fewer rows. |\n    80|| 7 | **Sort reduction**: `SORT` + slice-first-n → `TOPK`; sort after filters, not before; drop sorts whose order is later destroyed | 5–20% | med | TOPK = first n of the same stable SORT (doc). Ties are preserved because both are stable. |\n    81|| 8 | **Join algorithm choice** HJOIN ↔ NLJOIN by cost model | small-med | very low | Identical results by spec; only cost differs. Stats are fine here. |\n    82|| 9 | **Idiom rewrites** (pattern-matched, each behind a precise matcher): self-join + GROUP + GMAX → `GROUP/GMAX/GID/GATHER` (q6); \"count of better rows\" top-n per group → sort + rank (q3); join-then-dedup semi-join → dedup the right side first (q5) | 2–10× on those programs | **high** | Must match NULL semantics exactly: HJOIN drops NULL keys but GROUP keeps them, so filter out NULL keys explicitly; GMAX \"first of equals\" printing scale. Only enabled after the evaluator passes with 0 defects on targeted stress data. |\n    83|\n    84|**Rule: never trade correctness for cycles.** Each rewrite ships with a unit test (before/after program pair) plus targeted adversarial data.\n    85|\n    86|**VM-limit safety:** no rewrite may increase any register's maximum length or the total HJOIN/GROUP input (work limit). This is checked by the cost estimator.\n    87|\n    88|---\n    89|\n    90|## 4. Evaluator design (`./evaluate OPTIMIZER`)\n    91|\n    92|1. **Corpus (seeded, deterministic).**\n    93|   - The 8 example programs.\n    94|   - **Generated programs**: a template generator over the example schema that emits legacy-style plans: scan/filter/project, 1–4 joins along `refs`, group-aggregate, sort/topk/slice, string transforms (NULLIFE/RTRIM/UPPER/CAT/LEFT), dates, arithmetic, with deliberate bloat (wide fan-outs, late filters, dead columns, self-joins).\n    95|   - **Mutants of the examples** (swap predicates or literals, change sort keys or directions).\n    96|   - Programs are type-correct by construction, and are kept only if the original runs without error on at least one dataset.\n    97|2. **Data (per schema).** A constraint-respecting generator: unique `key`s, `refs` drawn from the parent key (plus NULLs where nullable), `check` bounds including boundaries, `sorted` order, `not_null`. It is adversarial: NULLs, ties, `'Open '`/`'OPEN'`/`'open'`, empty strings, empty tables, 1-row tables, duplicate join keys, NUM scale variants (`1.0` vs `1.00`), boundary dates. Every dataset is validated by `bin/minivm --schema` (it checks constraints), and its schema file is produced the same way.\n    98|3. **Run.** For each program: call `OPTIMIZER prog.mini schema.json` once (1 s timeout). Then run the original and optimized programs on K datasets (K≈8–12).\n    99|4. **Compare** with the rubric in §5. Skip pairs where the original errors.\n   100|5. **Report** defects with a minimal repro (program, optimized program, dataset, diff) saved to `eval_out/`. Exit 1 if there are any defects (or optimizer failures), else 0.\n   101|6. **Budget** [est from measurements]: ~60 programs × (1 optimizer call + 2×10 VM runs) ≈ 1,300 runs × 42 ms ÷ 16 workers ≈ 4–8 s, plus optimizer time ≤ 60 s worst case in parallel. A hard watchdog at 100 s stops new work, prints the report, and exits non-zero if any defect was found so far.\n   102|\n   103|**Evaluator self-test (meta-eval):**\n   104|- The identity optimizer (`cat`) must give 0 false alarms.\n   105|- A set of **known-bad mutant optimizers** must each be caught: drop a filter, flip `ASC`/`DESC`, drop `NULLEQ`, drop a tie-break sort key, replace `IS` with `EQ`, reorder unsorted output only (must *not* be flagged when order isn't specified), change NUM rounding, introduce DIV-by-zero on filtered rows.\n   106|- Recall = caught ÷ mutants. Target 100%.\n   107|\n   108|---\n   109|\n   110|## 5. Eval rubric\n   111|\n   112|**Outputs (per program × dataset):**\n   113|- **O1** `ncols` equal, and the optimized run succeeds whenever the original succeeds.\n   114|- **O2** Rows equal as a list if order is specified (Q1), else as a multiset (sort both by canonical key).\n   115|- **O3** Numbers (INT or NUM, parsed exactly via `Decimal`) satisfy `|a−b| ≤ 1e-6·max(|a|,|b|)` (`a==b` for 0). STR/DATE/BOOL are exact; NULL = NULL.\n   116|- **O4** The optimized program doesn't exceed VM limits or the 1 s optimizer limit.\n   117|- **O5** If the original errors, the pair is skipped (not a defect).\n   118|\n   119|**Programs (performance):**\n   120|- **P1** Cycles of optimized vs original per dataset: speedup ratio, plus a geomean over the corpus.\n   121|- **P2** Instruction count before and after.\n   122|- **P3** Peak register size and VM-limit headroom (never worse than the original).\n   123|- **P4** Optimizer wall time (max must be < 1 s).\n   124|- **P5** Regression flag: optimized cycles > original cycles on any dataset (allowed but reported; target zero).\n   125|\n   126|**Evaluator:**\n   127|- **E1** Defects caught on mutant optimizers (recall, target 100%).\n   128|- **E2** False alarms on the identity and correct optimizers (target 0).\n   129|- **E3** Wall time (< 120 s; target < 60 s).\n   130|- **E4** Determinism: the same seed gives the same verdict.\n   131|\n   132|---\n   133|\n   134|## 6. Stopping criteria for the build ↔ evaluate loop\n   135|\n   136|- **Success, stop:** 0 defects on the full eval with 3 different seeds; E1 = 100% and E2 = 0; geomean speedup ≥ 2× on examples [target est]; all optimizer calls < 1 s; evaluator < 2 min.\n   137|- **No more improvement, stop that rewrite:** two consecutive iterations where geomean cycles improve by < 3%, or a rewrite's gain doesn't justify its risk. Move to the next rank, or stop.\n   138|- **Budget used up, stop:** user time hits 2h45m, or the AI token budget reaches its cap (we track per session). Ship the last green commit.\n   139|- **Ask the user when:** a rewrite depends on an open-question interpretation (Q1/Q2); a defect can't be explained within 2 attempts; a fix requires dropping a rewrite that gives > 20% of the gain; or any destructive git action (history rewrite for binaries, §10).\n   140|- **Hard rule:** any defect is a red build. Revert or disable the rewrite before doing anything else.\n   141|\n   142|---\n   143|\n   144|## 7. Failure modes\n   145|\n   146|| Failure | Detection | Fix / prevention |\n   147||---|---|---|\n   148|| Rewrite changes NULL semantics (HJOIN vs GROUP NULL keys) | targeted NULL-heavy data; mutant tests | explicit NULL filters in idiom rewrites; per-rewrite unit tests |\n   149|| Rewrite introduces an error (DIV by 0, type error, out-of-range GATHER, DATEADD overflow) on rows the original skipped | O1 failures on adversarial data | the \"subset of evaluated rows\" rule (§3 #4) |\n   150|| Lost tie order (unstable reorder) | O2 on tie-heavy data | always preserve order; only stable sorts and IDX/ascending composition |\n   151|| Relying on stats instead of constraints | data generator deliberately violates stats (different ranges, distincts) | lint: the correctness path never reads `stats` |\n   152|| Order-insensitive comparison hides a real defect, or order-sensitive gives false alarms | meta-eval with \"reorder-only\" mutant | Q1 detector unit-tested on all 8 examples |\n   153|| NUM scale or rounding differences | O3 tolerance; DIV/MUL results compared via Decimal | don't reassociate arithmetic |\n   154|| Optimized program blows VM limits (join expansion) | O4; P3 report | cost check: never increase peak register size or HJOIN/GROUP input |\n   155|| Optimizer > 1 s on big programs (20k instructions) | timing in runner; a stress program with 20k lines | linear passes, iteration cap, 0.8 s deadline → fall back |\n   156|| Evaluator > 2 min | wall-time report | watchdog at 100 s; parallel pool; cap on corpus size |\n   157|| Generator makes invalid data | `bin/minivm --schema` rejects it | regenerate; count rejections in the report |\n   158|| Overfitting to 8 examples | held-out generated programs scored separately | rewrites must be general passes; idioms gated |\n   159|\n   160|---\n   161|\n   162|## 8. Each\nline holds one instruction. A `;` starts a comment, which runs to the end of\nthe line; a line may hold only a comment, or be blank. Spaces and tabs are\ninterchangeable: they separate the opcode from its operands, and may indent a\nline or surround an operand.\n\n```text\n; Ids and amounts of orders over 100.\nload   id, orders.o_id\nload   amt, orders.o_amt\ngt     m, amt, 100      ; NULL where o_amt is NULL\nidx    i, m\ngather a, id, i\ngather b, amt, i\nout    a, b\n```\n\nThe program must end with its only `OUT`; see [Program rules](running.md#program\n-rules).                                                                        \n## Instructions\n\nAn instruction is an opcode followed by comma-separated operands:\n\n```text\nOP dest, operand, ...\n```\n\nOpcodes are case-insensitive: `gt`, `Gt` and `GT` are the same instruction.\nSo are the keywords `NULL`, `TRUE`, `FALSE`, `ASC`, `DESC`, `NF`, `NL` and\n`NULLEQ`.\nEach opcode's operands are given on its page in the\n[instruction reference](instructions/README.md).\n\n## Registers\n\nRegister names are identifiers, such as `r1`, `amt` or `_t0`: a letter or `_`,\nfollowed by letters, digits and `_`. Register names are case-sensitive, and a\nkeyword can't be a register name. A register holds a column or a group set\n([Values](values.md#columns-and-group-sets)) and can be overwritten.\n\n## Operands\n\nAn operand is one of:\n\n| Operand | Example | Used by |\n|---|---|---|\n| register | `amt` | every instruction |\n| literal | `100.00` | element-wise instructions, `FILL`, integer operands such \nas `LEFT`'s `n` |                                                               | `table.column` | `orders.o_amt` | [`LOAD`](instructions/columns.md#load) |\n| sort key | `amt DESC NL` | [`SORT`, `TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys)\n |                                                                              | `NULLEQ` | `NULLEQ` | [`NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) \n|                                                                               \n## Literals\n\n| Literal | Type | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| `42`, `-7` | INT | must fit in 128 bits |\n| `12.50` | NUM | must be exact, in the [NUM range](values.md#num-range) |\n| `'it''s'` | STR | a quote inside the string is written twice |\n| `#2024-01-31#` | DATE | years 0001 to 9999 |\n| `NULL` | NULL | |\n| `TRUE`, `FALSE` | BOOL | |\n\nA literal stands for that value at every row.\n\n## Integer operands\n\nSome operands must be integer literals rather than registers: `n` and `len`\n(`LEFT`, `SUBSTR`, `SLICE`, `TOPK`) are non-negative, and `SUBSTR`'s `start` is\nat least 1. They may be arbitrarily large; a count larger than the input means\nall of it.\n=== values.md\n[MiniVM docs](README.md) › Values\n\n# Values\n\nThis page describes MiniVM's values and types, what a register holds, and how\nvalues are ordered and compared.\n\n## Types\n\n| Type | Values | Literal |\n|---|---|---|\n| INT | exact 128-bit integer; a result outside -2^127 .. 2^127-1 is an error | \n`42` |                                                                          | NUM | decimal: see [NUM range](#num-range) | `12.50` |\n| STR | string | `'it''s'` |\n| DATE | calendar date | `#2024-01-31#` |\n| BOOL | `FALSE` or `TRUE` | `TRUE` |\n\n`NULL` is a value of its own, written `NULL`. Unless an instruction says\notherwise, an element-wise result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`\n([element-wise instructions](instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions)).\n\nLiteral syntax is in [Literals](language.md#literals). Stored columns have\ntype INT, NUM, STR or DATE ([table sets](running.md#table-sets)).\n\n## NUM range\n\nA NUM is below 1e28 in magnitude and has at most 28 digits after the point,\nand its digits without the point, read as an integer, are at most\n2^96 - 1 = 79228162514264337593543950335: 28 or 29 significant digits.\nA NUM keeps its digits after the point, so `1.0` and `1.00` are equal but\nprint differently.\n\nA NUM literal or stored value must be such a number exactly; trailing zeros\nafter the point are dropped as far as needed. A NUM result is rounded half to\neven to the most digits after the point that fit, and a result of magnitude\n1e28 or more is the error `numeric overflow`. Where an INT meets a NUM in\narithmetic, and in `DIV`, an INT operand above 2^96 - 1 in magnitude is that\nerror too, even if the result would fit.\n\n## Columns and group sets\n\nA register holds either:\n\n- a **column**: a vector of values; or\n- a **group set**: a grouping of rows, made by\n  [`GROUP`](instructions/grouping.md#group) or [`GALL`](instructions/grouping.md\n#gall)                                                                            and read by the other [grouping instructions](instructions/grouping.md).\n\nRegisters can be overwritten.\n\n## Ordering\n\nThese instructions compare values:\n\n- [`EQ`, `NE`, `LT`, `LE`, `GT`, `GE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) \nand [`IS`](instructions/logic.md#is)                                            - [`SORT`](instructions/sorting.md#sort) and [`TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#to\npk)                                                                             - the joins [`NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin)\n- [`GMIN`, `GMAX`](instructions/grouping.md#gmin-gmax)\n\nThey order values as follows:\n\n| Values | Order |\n|---|---|\n| INT and NUM | by numeric value, exactly at any magnitude; INT and NUM mix |\n| STR | by bytes |\n| DATE | by date |\n| BOOL | `FALSE < TRUE` |\n\nComparing any other mix of types, such as STR with INT or DATE with NUM, is an\nerror.\n\nString comparison is exact: there is no case folding, and trailing spaces\ncount, so `'ab'` and `'ab '` differ, as do `'ab'` and `'AB'`.\n\nHow each instruction treats `NULL` is given on its page; for sorts, see\n[sort keys](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys).\n=== cycles.md\n[MiniVM docs](README.md) › Cycles\n\n# Cycles\n\nThis page defines how many cycles a program costs. A program's cost is the sum\nof its instructions' costs, and `bin/minivm` reports it as `cycles`\n([Running](running.md#command-line)).\n\n## Base cost\n\nEvery instruction costs 4, plus the cost given for it in the\n[cost table](#cost-table). `OUT` costs only the 4.\n\nA run is stopped with an error if it does too much work; see the\n[work limit](running.md#program-rules).\n\n## String bytes\n\nThe string bytes of a value are the number of bytes in it if it is a STR, and\n0 otherwise (including `NULL`).\n\nAn [element-wise instruction](instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions)\ncosts, for each element of its result, a base amount plus string bytes:\n\n| Instructions | Base per element |\n|---|---|\n| `DIV` `IDIV` `MOD` | 6 |\n| `TRUNC` `YEAR` `MONTH` `DAY` `DOW` `DATEADD` `DATEDIFF` | 2 |\n| every other element-wise instruction | 1 |\n\n| Instructions | String bytes per element |\n|---|---|\n| comparisons: `EQ` `NE` `LT` `LE` `GT` `GE` `IS` | the bytes of the shorter ope\nrand |                                                                          | `LEN` | the bytes of its operand |\n| `ISNULL` `NVL` `IF` `NULLIF` `NULLIFE` | nothing |\n| every other element-wise instruction | 1 per byte of each string operand (lite\nrals included) and of its result |                                              \nA literal operand counts at every element, like the value it stands for.\n\n## Comparisons\n\n`SORT` and `TOPK` compare rows on their sort keys\n([sort keys](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys)). One comparison of two rows\ncosts, for each key examined until one differs, 2 plus the bytes of the\nshorter string.\n\nFor example, on a table `t` whose STR column `s` and INT column `n` hold the\nrows `('ab', 5)` and `('ab', 7)`, comparing the two rows on keys\n`s ASC NL, n ASC NL` costs 2 + 2 for the first key, which is equal, and 2 + 0\nfor the second, which differs: 6 in all. Sorting the two rows takes that one\ncomparison:\n\n```text\nLOAD s, t.s\nLOAD n, t.n\nSORT o, s ASC NL, n ASC NL\nOUT  o\n```\n\ncosts (4 + 2) + (4 + 2) + (4 + 2 x 2 rows + 6) + 4 = 30 cycles.\n\n## 4 |\n| total | | 39 |\n\n`UPPER` pays for the bytes of its operand and of its result; `EQ` pays for the\nshorter of `u` and the literal `'AB'` at each row. `bin/minivm` prints\n`{\"ncols\":1,\"rows\":[[true],[false],[null]],\"cycles\":39}`.\n=== running.md\n[MiniVM docs](README.md) › Running\n\n# Running\n\nThis page gives the rules every program must follow, what happens on an error,\nhow to run a program with `bin/minivm`, and the JSON format of the tables it\nreads.\n\n## Program rules\n\nThe last instruction must be the program's only [`OUT`](instructions/columns.md#\nout).                                                                           \n| Limit | Value |\n|---|---|\n| instructions per program | at most 20,000 |\n| values held by one register | at most 4,000,000 (a join's output counts) |\n| values held by all registers together | at most 64,000,000; a long string coun\nts as several values (about 1 per 32 bytes) |                                   | work per run | roughly 300,000,000 [cycles](cycles.md); see below |\n| rows per table | at most 10,000 |\n| program file | at most 4 MiB |\n| table-set file | at most 32 MiB and 2,000,000 JSON values |\n\nThe work limit stops runaway programs. It counts a run's cycles, but `HJOIN`\nand `GROUP` and copying long strings use it up faster than their cycles\nsuggest, so such programs stop somewhat sooner. Exceeding it, like any other\nlimit, is an error. It has no effect on the cycles reported for a run that\nfinishes.\n\n## Errors\n\nAny error stops the program. No result is printed; the error goes to stderr\nand `bin/minivm` exits with status 1.\n\n## Command line\n\n```sh\nbin/minivm PROGRAM.mini TABLES.json\nbin/minivm --schema TABLES.json\n```\n\nruns the program in `PROGRAM.mini` on the [table set](#table-sets) in\n`TABLES.json`. On success it prints one line of JSON to stdout and exits 0:\n\n```json\n{\"ncols\": N, \"rows\": [...], \"cycles\": C}\n```\n\n- `ncols` is the number of `OUT` operands.\n- `rows` is the result, one array of `ncols` values per row.\n  `NULL` is `null` and a BOOL is `true` or `false`. An INT is a JSON integer,\n  or a string of its digits outside -2^63 .. 2^63-1. A NUM is a string that keep\ns                                                                                 its digits after the point (`\"250.00\"`), a STR a string, and a DATE a string\n  `\"YYYY-MM-DD\"`.\n- `cycles` is the program's cost ([Cycles](cycles.md)).\n\n| Exit status | Meaning |\n|---|---|\n| 0 | success; the result is on stdout |\n| 1 | error; the message is on stderr |\n| 2 | wrong number of arguments; a usage line is on stderr |\n\nWith the program from [Language](language.md#programs) saved as\n`over100.mini` and the [example table set](#example) as `orders.json`:\n\n```sh\n$ bin/minivm over100.mini orders.json\n{\"ncols\":2,\"rows\":[[1,\"250.00\"]],\"cycles\":42}\n```\n\n`bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json` prints the table set's [schema file](#schema-f\niles)                                                                           as one line of JSON instead of running a program.\n\nA program that compares a DATE with an INT stops with an error:\n\n```text\nLOAD d, orders.o_date\nGT   m, d, 5\nOUT  m\n```\n\n```sh\n$ bin/minivm bad.mini orders.json\nerror: line 2: GT: expected a number, got DATE\n```\n\n## Table sets\n\nA table set is a JSON object mapping each table name to its columns and rows:\n\n```json\n{\"<table>\": {\"columns\": [{\"name\": \"c\", \"type\": \"INT|NUM|STR|DATE\"}], \"rows\": [[.\n..], ...]}}                                                                     ```\n\n- Table and column names are identifiers (letters, digits and `_`, not starting\n  with a digit), compared without regard to case. Duplicate names are an error.\n- `columns` lists each column's `name` and `type`, one of `INT`, `NUM`, `STR`, `\nDATE`.                                                                          - `rows` lists each row as an array of values, one per column, in column order.\n  A table without `rows` is empty.\n- A table may also declare [constraints](#constraints).\n- Any key other than those shown or listed there is an error, as is a repeated k\ney.                                                                             - A table holds at most 10,000 rows.\n- INT values are JSON integers that fit in 32 bits.\n- NUM values may be JSON numbers or strings. They must be exact, in the\n  [NUM range](values.md#num-range).\n- Dates are strings `\"YYYY-MM-DD\"`, years 0001 to 9999.\n- JSON `null` is `NULL`.\n\nA program reads a stored column with `LOAD d, table.column` ([`LOAD`](instructio\nns/columns.md#load)).                                                           \n### Constraints\n\nA table may declare what its rows guarantee. `bin/minivm` checks every declared\nconstraint when it reads the table set, and a table set that breaks one is an er\nror.                                                                            \n| Key | Example | Guarantee |\n|---|---|---|\n| `key` | `[\"l_order\", \"l_no\"]` | the columns are never `NULL`, and no two rows \nagree on all of them |                                                          | `not_null` | `[\"p_price\"]` | the columns are never `NULL` |\n| `refs` | `{\"l_prod\": \"products.p_id\"}` | every non-NULL value of the column is\n a value of the other column, which must be its table's whole `key` and have the same type (INT and NUM may refer to each other) |                              | `check` | `{\"l_qty\": [1, 500]}` | every non-NULL value lies between the bounds\n, inclusive; `null` leaves a side open; INT, NUM and DATE columns only |        | `sorted` | `[\"l_order\", \"l_no\"]` | the rows are stored in ascending order of t\nhe columns, as `ASC NF` sorts them |                                            \nValues are compared as in [Ordering](values.md#ordering), so NUM keys `1.0` and\n`1.00` are the same key. Column names in constraints are compared without regard\nto case, and naming a column twice in one constraint is an error. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                    \n   238|| Instruction | Result |\n   239||---|---|\n   240|| [`LOAD d, table.column`](#load) | the column as stored |\n   241|| [`FILL d, lit, s`](#fill) | `lit` repeated once per value of `s` |\n   242|| [`IOTA d, s`](#iota) | positions `0 .. len(s)-1` |\n   243|| [`IDX d, s`](#idx) | positions where `s` is TRUE |\n   244|| [`GATHER d, s, i`](#gather) | `d[k] = s[i[k]]` |\n   245|| [`SLICE d, s, n`](#slice) | the first `n` values of `s` |\n   246|| [`OUT s, ...`](#out) | the program's result |\n   247|\n   248|## `LOAD`\n   249|\n   250|```text\n   251|LOAD d, table.column\n   252|```\n   253|\n   254|Sets `d` to the column `column` of table `table` as stored. An empty string stay\n   255|s `''`; it is not NULL.                                                         \n   256|**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.\n   257|\n   258|## `FILL`\n   259|\n   260|```text\n   261|FILL d, lit, s\n   262|```\n   263|\n   264|Sets `d` to the literal `lit` repeated once per value of `s`. `lit` must be a li\n   265|teral.                                                                          \n   266|**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.\n   267|\n   268|## `IOTA`\n   269|\n   270|```text\n   271|IOTA d, s\n   272|```\n   273|\n   274|Sets `d` to the positions `0 .. len(s)-1` of `s`.\n   275|\n   276|**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.\n   277|\n   278|## `IDX`\n   279|\n   280|```text\n   281|IDX d, s\n   282|```\n   283|\n   284|Sets `d` to the positions, in order, where the BOOL column `s` is TRUE. FALSE an\n   285|d NULL positions are left out.                                                  \n   286|**Cycles:** 1 per input value.\n   287|\n   288|## `GATHER`\n   289|\n   290|```text\n   291|GATHER d, s, i\n   292|```\n   293|\n   294|Sets `d[k] = s[i[k]]` for every position `k` of `i`; `d` has the length of `i`. \n   295|Every index must be an INT in range for `s`, or the instruction is an error. Use it with the positions from [`IDX`](#idx), [`SORT`](sorting.md#sort), [`TOPK`](sorting.md#topk), the [joins](joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) and [`GFIRST`](grouping.md#gfirst) to filter, reorder, pair up or pick rows.                                \n   296|**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.\n   297|\n   298|## `SLICE`\n   299|\n   300|```text\n   301|SLICE d, s, n\n   302|```\n   303|\n   304|Sets `d` to the first `n` values of `s` (all of `s` if it has fewer). `n` is an \n   305|integer literal.                                                                \n   306|**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.\n   307|\n   308|## `OUT`\n   309|\n   310|```text\n   311|OUT s, ...\n   312|```\n   313|\n   314|Produces the program's result: one column per operand, all the same length. `OUT\n   315|` must be the last instruction and the program's only `OUT` ([program rules](../running.md#program-rules)).                                                     \n   316|**Cycles:** nothing beyond the base cost.\n   317|=== dates.md\n   318|[MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Dates\n   319|\n   320|# Dates\n   321|\n   322|Element-wise operations on DATE values. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                           \n   379|| Instruction | Result |\n   380||---|---|\n   381|| [`GROUP g, k, ...`](#group) | group set: rows with equal keys share a group |\n   382|| [`GALL g, s`](#gall) | group set: one group holding every row of `s` |\n   383|| [`GID d, g`](#gid) | group number of each row |\n   384|| [`GFIRST d, g`](#gfirst) | position of each group's first row |\n   385|| [`GCOUNT d, g`](#gcount) | rows per group |\n   386|| [`GCOUNTV d, g, s`](#gcountv) | non-NULL values of `s` per group |\n   387|| [`GSUM d, g, s`](#gsum) | sum of non-NULL values per group |\n   388|| [`GMIN d, g, s` / `GMAX`](#gmin-gmax) | least / greatest non-NULL value per gr\n   389|oup |                                                                           \n   390|## Group sets\n   391|\n   392|A register holds either a column or a group set ([values](../values.md#columns-a\n   393|nd-group-sets)). A group set assigns each of its rows a group number; groups are numbered from 0 in order of first appearance. [`GROUP`](#group) and [`GALL`](#gall) produce a group set. [`GID`](#gid) returns a column with one value per row; the aggregates [`GFIRST`](#gfirst) through [`GMAX`](#gmin-gmax) return a column with one value per group, the value for group `k` at position `k`. The `s` operand of an aggregate is a column over the same rows as the group set; a different length is an error.                                                            \n   394|Aggregate columns of the same group set line up with each other. To label each g\n   395|roup with its key, gather the key at [`GFIRST`](#gfirst). Orders per status:    \n   396|```text\n   397|LOAD   st, orders.o_status\n   398|GROUP  g, st\n   399|GFIRST f, g\n   400|GATHER key, st, f\n   401|GCOUNT n, g\n   402|OUT    key, n\n   403|```\n   404|\n   405|On `examples/data.json` this prints `[[\"open\",7],[\"closed\",12],[\"shipped\",11]]`.\n   406|\n   407|## `GROUP`\n   408|\n   409|```text\n   410|GROUP g, k, ...\n   411|```\n   412|\n   413|Sets `g` to a group set over the rows of the key columns `k, ...`: rows with equ\n   414|al keys share a group, and NULL equals NULL. All key columns must have the same length. Keys are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering): INT and NUM mix (`1` and `1.00` share a group), and a key column holding values that can't be compared (e.g. STR and INT) is an error.                                       \n   415|**Cycles:** per row: 6 plus the string bytes of its keys ([rules](../cycles.md#s\n   416|tring-bytes)).                                                                  \n   417|## `GALL`\n   418|\n   419|```text\n   420|GALL g, s\n   421|```\n   422|\n   423|Sets `g` to a group set with one group holding every row of `s`, even when `s` i\n   424|s empty.                                                                        \n   425|**Cycles:** 1 per row.\n   426|\n   427|## `GID`\n   428|\n   429|```text\n   430|GID d, g\n   431|```\n   432|\n   433|Sets `d` to the group number of each row of `g`.\n   434|\n   435|**Cycles:** 1 per row.\n   436|\n   437|## `GFIRST`\n   438|\n   439|```text\n   440|GFIRST d, g\n   441|```\n   442|\n   443|Sets `d` to the position of each group's first row. The result is NULL for the g\n   444|roup of an empty `GALL`.                                                        \n   445|**Cycles:** 1 per row.\n   446|\n   447|## `GCOUNT`\n   448|\n   449|```text\n   450|GCOUNT d, g\n   451|```\n   452|\n   453|Sets `d` to the number of rows in each group.\n   454|\n   455|**Cycles:** 2 per row.\n   456|\n   457|## `GCOUNTV`\n   458|\n   459|```text\n   460|GCOUNTV d, g, s\n   461|```\n   462|\n   463|Sets `d` to the number of non-NULL values of `s` in each group.\n   464|\n   465|**Cycles:** 2 per row.\n   466|\n   467|## `GSUM`\n   468|\n   469|```text\n   470|GSUM d, g, s\n   471|```\n   472|\n   473|Sets `d` to the sum of the non-NULL values of `s` in each group: INT when all ar\n   474|e INT, else NUM. The result is NULL for a group with no non-NULL values. A NUM sum is computed exactly, with as many digits after the point as the value with the most, and rounded once as in [NUM range](../values.md#num-range), so it doesn't depend on the order of the rows. Only each group's total is checked: a total outside the INT or NUM range is the error `numeric overflow`, whatever the running sums along the way.                                                           \n   475|**Cycles:** 2 per row.\n   476|\n   477|## `GMIN`, `GMAX`\n   478|\n   479|```text\n   480|GMIN d, g, s\n   481|GMAX d, g, s\n   482|```\n   483|\n   484|Sets `d` to the least (`GMIN`) or greatest (`GMAX`) non-NULL value of `s` in eac\n   485|h group, the first of equals: of `1`, `1.0` and `1.00`, whichever comes first. Values are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering). The result is NULL for a group with no non-NULL values.                                             \n   486|**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus the bytes of each non-NULL string ([rules](../cycles\n   487|.md#string-bytes)).                                                             === joins.md\n   488|[MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Joins\n   489|\n   490|# Join instructions\n   491|\n   492|`NLJOIN` and `HJOIN` pair up the rows of two key columns whose keys are equal an\n   493|d return the pairs as two position columns. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                                                  \n   494|| Instruction | Result |\n   495||---|---|\n   496|| [`NLJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]`](#nljoin-hjoin) | positions of all pairs w\n   497|ith `lk[i] = rk[j]` |                                                           | [`HJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]`](#nljoin-hjoin) | same result as `NLJOIN` |\n   498|\n   499|## `NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`\n   500|\n   501|```text\n   502|NLJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]\n   503|HJOIN  li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]\n   504|```\n   505|\n   506|Finds all pairs `(i, j)` with `lk[i] = rk[j]`, ordered by `i` then `j`. Sets `li\n   507|` to the positions into `lk` and `ri` to the positions into `rk`, one entry per pair; if `li` and `ri` are the same register, it holds the positions into `rk`. Keys are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering): a non-NULL left key that can't be compared with a non-NULL right key (e.g. STR with INT) is an error. A NULL key matches no key, unless the optional `NULLEQ` flag is given, in which case NULL keys match each other. `HJOIN` gives the same result as `NLJOIN`, errors included; only the cost differs.                                            \n   508|**Cycles (`NLJOIN`):** per pair of rows: 1 plus the bytes of the shorter string \n   509|key ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)); plus 2 per output pair.               \n   510|**Cycles (`HJOIN`):** per row of either side: 6 plus its key's string bytes ([ru\n   511|les](../cycles.md#string-bytes)); plus 2 per output pair.                       \n   512|### Example\n   513|\n   514|[`GATHER`](columns.md#gather) through `li` picks columns of the left rows and th\n   515|rough `ri` columns of the right rows, giving one row per pair. Customers with their region's name:                                                              \n   516|```text\n   517|LOAD   reg, customers.c_region\n   518|LOAD   code, regions.r_code\n   519|HJOIN  li, ri, reg, code\n   520|LOAD   cname, customers.c_name\n   521|LOAD   rname, regions.r_name\n   522|GATHER c, cname, li\n   523|GATHER r, rname, ri\n   524|OUT    c, r\n   525|```\n   526|\n   527|On `examples/data.json` this prints `[[\"Cy\",\"Southern\"],[\"Dee\",\"West Coast\"],[\"E\n   528|ve\",\"Southern\"], ...]`.                                                         === logic.md\n   529|[MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Logic\n   530|\n   531|# Logic\n   532|\n   533|Element-wise comparisons, BOOL logic and NULL handling. All instructions on this\n   534| page follow the [element-wise rules](README.md#element-wise-instructions); where an instruction's NULL behavior differs from the default (the result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`), its section says so.                               \n   535|| Instruction | Result |\n   536||---|---|\n   537|| [`EQ` `NE` `LT` `LE` `GT` `GE` `d, a, b`](#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) | BOOL compariso\n   538|n |                                                                             | [`IS d, a, b`](#is) | BOOL, never NULL: equal, or both NULL |\n   539|| [`AND d, a, b`](#and-or) / `OR` | three-valued logic |\n   540|| [`NOT d, a`](#not) | BOOL negation |\n   541|| [`ISNULL d, a`](#isnull) | BOOL, never NULL |\n   542|| [`NVL d, a, b`](#nvl) | `a`, or `b` when `a` is NULL |\n   543|| [`IF d, c, a, b`](#if) | `a` where `c` is TRUE, else `b` |\n   544|| [`NULLIF d, a, b`](#nullif) | NULL where `a IS b`, else `a` |\n   545|| [`NULLIFE d, a`](#nullife) | NULL where `a` is the empty string, else `a` |\n   546|\n   547|## `EQ`, `NE`, `LT`, `LE`, `GT`, `GE`\n   548|\n   549|```text\n   550|EQ d, a, b\n   551|NE d, a, b\n   552|LT d, a, b\n   553|LE d, a, b\n   554|GT d, a, b\n   555|GE d, a, b\n   556|```\n   557|\n   558|BOOL comparison of `a` with `b`: `a = b`, `a <> b`, `a < b`, `a <= b`, `a > b`, \n   559|`a >= b`. Values are ordered as described in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering); comparing other mixes of types is an error.                                     \n   560|**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus the bytes of the shorter operand ([rules](../cyc\n   561|les.md#string-bytes)).                                                          \n   562|## `IS`\n   563|\n   564|```text\n   565|IS d, a, b\n   566|```\n   567|\n   568|BOOL, never NULL: TRUE where `a` and `b` are equal, or both NULL, and FALSE wher\n   569|e just one is NULL. Values are ordered as described in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering); comparing two non-NULL values of other mixes of types is an error.    \n   570|**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus the bytes of the shorter operand ([rules](../cyc\n   571|les.md#string-bytes)).                                                          \n   572|## `AND`, `OR`\n   573|\n   574|```text\n   575|AND d, a, b\n   576|OR  d, a, b\n   577|```\n   578|\n   579|Three-valued logic on BOOL values; GSUM uses the most decimal places in the group, and `MUL x, 1.000` changes how the result prints.\n   - **Other traps:** UPPER can change string length; customers and regions have no key, so joins to them can multiply rows; a `check` without `not_null` doesn't make a predicate always true; VM size limits can make a rewrite fail where the original ran.\n4. **Recommended order:** dead code and duplicate removal, then column fetching, then moving ops after filters, then sorts, then filter pushdown, then constraint rewrites, then join choice, then the self-join idioms last. The one global safety rule: an op may only run on a subset of the rows it ran on originally, in the same order, unless it provably can't fail.\n5. **Gate or skip:** turn on the idioms and join elimination only after the evaluator shows 0 defects on data heavy in NULLs, ties, mixed decimal places and empty tables. Skip arithmetic simplification, join reordering, and any use of stats for correctness. If the estimated cost isn't lower, or any intermediate would grow, output the original program unchanged.", "message_id": "5391261993809634"}], "model": "claude-opus-5-5", "thinkingEffort": "medium", "createdOn": 1794344175055, "summaryRevision": "", "autoRouterSelected": false}
